blocks.text: Module 3 was about getting data into KimTay's tables and pulling it back out. Module 4 is about asking sharper questions. Every query in this lesson reads a single table, which keeps the moving parts small while you learn the clauses that do the real filtering work.

A query is a question you put to the database in a form it can answer. The shape you already know is `SELECT` (which columns you want), `FROM` (which table they live in), and optionally `WHERE` (which rows qualify). Everything in this lesson is a refinement of those three lines.
**Start with the data:** this is the complete `ITEM` table used by the first examples. Read its five rows before looking at the first query.

blocks.caption: Source table: ITEM — all columns and all five rows

blocks.label: What you are building on
blocks.text: You already have `SELECT`, `FROM`, a `WHERE` with one comparison, and `ORDER BY`. This lesson adds compound conditions, ranges, arithmetic, pattern matching, and value lists. None of it replaces what you know; all of it plugs into the same statement.
4-1a Retrieving Certain Columns and All Rows

Start with the most common request a business makes: give me a few facts about everything. KimTay's bookkeeper wants an ID, a description, and a price for every item in stock, and nothing else. Name the columns you want, separated by commas, in the order you want to read them.

SELECT ITEM_ID, DESCRIPTION, PRICE
FROM ITEM;

That returns all five `ITEM` rows and exactly three columns. Two separate decisions produced that result: naming three columns is what limited the width, and leaving out `WHERE` is what kept every row.

blocks.caption: Result of the three-column query against ITEM (prices shown as they are stored)

blocks.label: Why the sandbox drops trailing zeros
blocks.text: MySQL prints a `DECIMAL(7,2)` column with both decimal places, so `PRICE` reads 42.50 and a zero balance reads 0.00. The browser engine on this page prints the shortest form of the same number, so you will see 42.5, and 0 instead of 0.00, and 7500 instead of 7500.00. The stored value is identical; only the printing differs. Tables in this lesson show the stored form.

The order of the names in the `SELECT` list is the order of the columns in the result. If the warehouse manager wants the description on the left, write `SELECT DESCRIPTION, ITEM_ID, PRICE FROM ITEM;` and you get the same five rows rearranged. Nothing about the stored table changes.
4-1b Retrieving All Columns and All Rows
When you want every column, you can list all six by name, or use the shorthand asterisk.

SELECT *
FROM ITEM;

That returns the same five rows with all six columns, in the order they were defined in `CREATE TABLE`: `ITEM_ID`, `DESCRIPTION`, `CATEGORY`, `ON_HAND`, `PRICE`, `REORDER_LEVEL`. The asterisk is not a chooser and it is not a wildcard for rows; it means every column.

blocks.label: Fine for exploring, risky in a saved script
blocks.text: `SELECT *` is the fastest way to look around a table you do not know yet. In a script you plan to keep, name the columns. If the table is ever rebuilt with an extra column, `SELECT *` silently changes what your report returns, while a named list keeps returning what you asked for.

blocks.starter:
-- This returns three columns for all five items.
SELECT ITEM_ID, DESCRIPTION, PRICE
FROM ITEM;

-- Your turn: change it so that every column comes back, then run it again.
blocks.hint: Five rows either way; only the number of columns should change, from three to six.

blocks.text: 4-1c Using a WHERE Clause

Most business questions are about some rows, not all of them. A `WHERE` clause states a condition, and the engine keeps only the rows for which that condition is true. You have used `WHERE` with a single equality. Here is the full set of comparison operators.

blocks.caption: Comparison operators you can use in a condition

blocks.text: KimTay's warehouse manager wants a short list of the items running thin. Anything under 25 on hand is worth a look.
Two rows come back: AV07 with 15 on hand and GR15 with 22. The other three items hold 30, 48, and 120, so the condition is false for them and the engine drops them.
Conditions on text look the same, with one difference: the value goes inside single quotes.
That returns two rows: 1120 Access Pet Center and 1310 Companion Care Clinic.

blocks.label: Quote text, leave numbers bare
blocks.text: Character values need single quotes: `CITY = 'Maple Grove'`. Numeric values do not: `ON_HAND < 25`. Leave the quotes off a word and the engine reads it as a name, not as text, and refuses to run the statement. Watch out too for columns that look numeric but are not -- `CUSTOMER_NUM` is declared `CHAR(4)`, so it is text, and you write `WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '1120'` to get Access Pet Center.
`<>` is the not-equal operator. Both MySQL and SQLite also accept `!=`, but `<>` is the standard spelling and works everywhere, so prefer it.
Three rows come back: CF21 in Food, DG04 in Accessory, and GR15 in Grooming. The two Habitat items, AV07 and FT88, are excluded.

items.title: Name the table
items.body: Decide which single table holds the fact you are filtering on, and put it after `FROM`.

items.title: Pick the column
items.body: Find the column that stores the value you care about. `ON_HAND` for stock levels, `CITY` for location, `CATEGORY` for kind of item.

items.title: Choose the operator
items.body: Equality for an exact match, `<` or `>` for a threshold, `<>` for everything except one value.

items.title: Write the value in the column's own form
items.body: Single quotes for character columns, bare digits for numeric columns.

items.title: Read the row count before you trust it
items.body: If a five-row table gives back five rows, your condition probably is not filtering anything. Check it against the data by hand.

blocks.text: The right side of a condition does not have to be a fixed value. It can be another column in the same row. `SELECT ITEM_ID, DESCRIPTION FROM ITEM WHERE ON_HAND < REORDER_LEVEL;` asks which items have fallen below their own reorder point. Against the current data it returns no rows at all, and that is the answer: nothing needs reordering today. An empty result is not an error.
4-1d Using Compound Conditions

Real questions usually carry more than one requirement. "Maple Grove customers who owe us money" is two conditions at once. You join simple conditions with `AND` and `OR`, and you flip one with `NOT`.

blocks.label: Compound condition
blocks.text: A condition built from two or more simple conditions joined by `AND` or `OR`, and optionally reversed by `NOT`. `AND` keeps a row only when every part is true. `OR` keeps a row when at least one part is true.

SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, BALANCE
FROM CUSTOMER
WHERE CITY = 'Maple Grove'
  AND BALANCE > 1000;
One row comes back: 1120 Access Pet Center, with a balance of 3512.50. Companion Care Clinic is also in Maple Grove, but its balance is 0.00, so it fails the second half and `AND` drops it.

SELECT ITEM_ID, DESCRIPTION, PRICE
FROM ITEM
WHERE CATEGORY = 'Food'
   OR PRICE > 60;
Two rows come back: AV07 at 64.99, which qualifies on price alone, and CF21 at 42.50, which qualifies on category alone. Neither row has to satisfy both halves, because `OR` asks for at least one.
That returns CF21, DG04, and GR15 -- the same three rows as `CATEGORY <> 'Habitat'`. `NOT` earns its keep in front of a longer condition, where there is no single operator to reverse.

blocks.label: Parentheses change the answer
blocks.text: When you mix `AND` and `OR` in one clause, `AND` is evaluated first. That is the single most common source of a query that runs cleanly and returns the wrong rows. Put parentheses around the part you want grouped, every time, even when you think you do not need them.

cards.title: Without parentheses: 2 rows
cards.body: `WHERE CATEGORY = 'Habitat' OR CATEGORY = 'Food' AND PRICE < 30` reads as Habitat OR (Food AND under 30). Both Habitat items pass untested on price, so AV07 at 64.99 and FT88 at 27.75 come back. CF21 is Food at 42.50, so it fails.

cards.title: With parentheses: 1 row
cards.body: `WHERE (CATEGORY = 'Habitat' OR CATEGORY = 'Food') AND PRICE < 30` reads as (Habitat or Food) AND under 30. Now the price test applies to all three of those items, and only FT88 at 27.75 survives.

blocks.starter:
-- Run this as written and count the rows.
SELECT ITEM_ID, CATEGORY, PRICE
FROM ITEM
WHERE CATEGORY = 'Habitat' OR CATEGORY = 'Food' AND PRICE < 30;

-- Now add parentheses so that the price test applies to both categories.
blocks.hint: Two rows before the parentheses, one row after. If both runs match, the parentheses landed in the wrong place.

blocks.text: 4-1e Using the BETWEEN Operator

Range questions come up constantly: prices in a window, dates in a month, balances in a band. You can always write a range as two conditions joined by `AND`, and `BETWEEN` is a shorter way to say the same thing. KimTay's buyer wants every item priced from 15.25 through 27.75.
Two rows come back: FT88 at 27.75 and GR15 at 15.25. Notice that both of those prices sit exactly on a boundary, and both matched.

blocks.label: BETWEEN includes both endpoints
blocks.text: `PRICE BETWEEN 15.25 AND 27.75` means exactly `PRICE >= 15.25 AND PRICE <= 27.75`. It adds no power to SQL, only readability. Two rules follow: write the low value first, because `BETWEEN 27.75 AND 15.25` can never be true and returns an empty result without complaining; and if you need an exclusive edge, write the comparisons out with `>` or `<` instead.
Same two rows, FT88 and GR15. Use whichever version reads more clearly to the next person who opens your script.

blocks.starter:
-- StayWell's leasing office wants every room renting from 450 through 610 a month.
SELECT PROPERTY_ID, ROOM_NUM, ROOM_TYPE, MONTHLY_RENT
FROM ROOM
WHERE MONTHLY_RENT BETWEEN 450 AND 610;

-- Your turn: rewrite the condition using >= and <= and confirm you get the same rooms.
blocks.hint: Four of the five rooms qualify; only the 725.00 studio in Sycamore Court falls outside the window. The rents print as 595 and 450 here, without the trailing zeros.

blocks.text: 4-1f Using Computed Columns

Some numbers a business needs are not stored anywhere. KimTay stores `ON_HAND` and `PRICE`, but nobody stores the value of the stock on the shelf, because it would go stale the moment either number changed. You calculate it in the query instead.

blocks.label: Computed column
blocks.text: A column that appears in the result but does not exist in the table. The engine works it out for each row from values that do exist, using `+`, `-`, `*`, and `/`. Nothing is written back to the table.

SELECT ITEM_ID, DESCRIPTION, ON_HAND * PRICE AS ON_HAND_VALUE
FROM ITEM;

blocks.caption: Value of the stock on hand, calculated per row, as each engine prints it

blocks.text: Read the AV07 row twice, because it is the interesting one. MySQL multiplies `DECIMAL` values exactly and reports 974.85. The browser engine on this page converts `DECIMAL` to binary floating point, where 64.99 has no exact representation, so 15 * 64.99 comes back as 974.8499999999999. Rounded to cents the two agree, and your query is correct in both.

blocks.label: Money and binary floating point
blocks.text: A long tail such as 974.8499999999999 in the sandbox is the storage format showing through, not a mistake in your arithmetic. It is also the reason production systems keep money in an exact type such as `DECIMAL` rather than a floating-point type, and the reason you round money for display rather than trusting the raw digits.

blocks.label: Always name a computed column
blocks.text: Without `AS`, the heading is whatever the engine decides to call the expression, and it differs between systems. `AS ON_HAND_VALUE` gives it a stable name you can rely on in a report. Keep alias names to one word with underscores: MySQL quotes identifiers with backticks while standard SQL uses double quotes, so a one-word alias saves you from having to choose.
Arithmetic works on any numeric columns, including two columns from the same row. KimTay's credit manager wants to know how much room each customer has left.

SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, CREDIT_LIMIT - BALANCE AS AVAILABLE_CREDIT
FROM CUSTOMER;

All four customers come back: 1120 with 3987.50 available, 1225 with 3800.00, 1310 with the full 10000.00, and 1420 with 1179.25. These subtractions land on exact cents in both engines, so the only difference you will see on this page is the missing trailing zeros.

Two rows come back: 1120 at 3987.50 and 1310 at 10000.00. Notice that the whole expression is repeated in the `WHERE` clause rather than the alias being reused. That is deliberate, and it is a real difference between engines: the browser engine on this page would accept `WHERE AVAILABLE_CREDIT > 3900`, while MySQL rejects an alias in `WHERE`. Repeating the expression runs everywhere.

blocks.starter:
-- Stock value per item, calculated on the fly.
SELECT ITEM_ID, DESCRIPTION, ON_HAND * PRICE AS ON_HAND_VALUE
FROM ITEM;

-- Your turn: write a query on CUSTOMER that shows CUSTOMER_NUM and
-- the credit still available (CREDIT_LIMIT minus BALANCE), keeping only
-- the customers with more than 3900 available.
blocks.hint: Two customers qualify. Repeat the whole expression in the WHERE clause instead of using the alias, so the query also runs on MySQL.

blocks.text: 4-1g Using the LIKE Operator
Equality is all-or-nothing: `STREET = '77 Elm St.'` finds one exact value and misses everything close to it. When you only know part of the value, use `LIKE` with a pattern.

blocks.label: Wildcard
blocks.text: A character in a pattern that stands for other characters. `%` stands for any run of characters, including none at all. `_` stands for exactly one character. Everything else in the pattern has to match literally.

blocks.caption: Patterns and what they find in the KimTay data
rows: four characters, F in second place

blocks.text: Two rows come back: 1225 at 642 Chestnut St. and 1420 at 77 Elm St. The leading `%` absorbs the house number and the street name, and because the pattern ends right after `St.`, the match is anchored to the end of the value.
Two rows: FT88 Fish Tank Filter Kit and GR15 Small Animal Grooming Kit. Move that percent sign to the other end and you would be asking for descriptions that start with Kit, which no item does.
One row: CF21. The pattern is four characters long, so it can only match a four-character ID, and the `F` is pinned to the second position. FT88 has its F first, so it does not qualify.

blocks.label: Two things to know before you rely on LIKE
blocks.text: First, letter case. As configured here, both MySQL and the browser engine ignore case for these ASCII values, so `'%cat%'` and `'%Cat%'` behave alike; other systems and other collations do not, so match the case you see in the data. Second, speed. A pattern that starts with `%` forces the engine to examine every row, which costs nothing on five items and a great deal on five million.

blocks.starter:
-- Customers whose street address ends in St.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, STREET
FROM CUSTOMER
WHERE STREET LIKE '%St.';

-- Your turn: change the pattern to find streets that contain Ave. anywhere.
blocks.hint: One customer qualifies. A percent sign on both sides is what says anywhere in the value, rather than only at the end.

blocks.text: 4-1h Using the IN Operator
The last shorthand in this lesson handles the question "is this column any one of these values?" KimTay's bookkeeper is preparing a mailing for the customers in Maple Grove and Brookville.
Three rows come back: 1120 and 1310 in Maple Grove, and 1420 in Brookville. Only 1225, in Northfield, is left out.

Identical three rows. `IN` is shorthand for that `OR` chain, and it gets easier to read the longer the list grows. The values inside the parentheses follow the same quoting rules as anywhere else: quotes for character columns, bare digits for numeric ones.

blocks.label: IN is a list, so it pairs with OR and never with AND
blocks.text: A common wrong turn is `WHERE CITY = 'Maple Grove' AND CITY = 'Brookville'`, which asks for rows whose one city value is two cities at once. It returns nothing, with no error to warn you. If you find yourself writing `AND` between two tests on the same column, you almost certainly want `IN`.
Put `NOT` in front of `IN` to exclude a list instead of including it.

Two rows come back: DG04 in Accessory and GR15 in Grooming. Later, in lesson 4-4, you will see that the list inside `IN` can be produced by another query instead of typed by hand. The operator behaves the same way; only the source of the values changes.

blocks.starter:
-- Items in either of two categories, written the long way.
SELECT ITEM_ID, DESCRIPTION, CATEGORY
FROM ITEM
WHERE CATEGORY = 'Food' OR CATEGORY = 'Grooming';

-- Your turn: rewrite the condition with IN and confirm the rows are the same.
blocks.hint: Two rows either way, CF21 and GR15. If you get five rows, check that the list is inside one pair of parentheses.

items: Name the columns you want in the `SELECT` list; keep `SELECT *` for exploring, not for scripts you save
Quote character values in single quotes and leave numeric values bare, even when a character column looks numeric
Use parentheses whenever `AND` and `OR` appear in the same `WHERE` clause
Write `BETWEEN` with the low value first, and remember that both endpoints are included
Give every computed column an alias with `AS`, and repeat the expression rather than the alias in `WHERE` so the query runs on MySQL too
Expect a computed money column to show a floating-point tail such as 974.8499999999999 in this page's sandbox; MySQL prints the exact 974.85
Reach for `LIKE` when you know part of a text value, and remember `%` is any run of characters while `_` is exactly one
Reach for `IN` when one column has to match any value in a list, and never join those tests with `AND`
Check the row count against the data by hand before you trust a new query; an empty result is an answer, not an error

quizzes.heading: Knowledge check: columns, rows, and a first WHERE

questions.scenarioTitle: The report with three columns too many
questions.stem: KimTay's bookkeeper asks for the ID, description, and price of every item in the ITEM table, and nothing else. A classmate hands back a result with all six columns in it. Which statement produces exactly what she asked for?
options: SELECT * FROM ITEM; because the asterisk lets you choose which of the columns come back
SELECT ITEM_ID, DESCRIPTION, PRICE; because FROM is optional once you name the columns
SELECT ITEM_ID, DESCRIPTION, PRICE FROM ITEM; the list picks columns, no WHERE keeps all rows
SELECT ITEM_ID, DESCRIPTION, PRICE FROM ITEM WHERE ITEM_ID = '*'; to sweep in every row
optionNotes: The asterisk is not a chooser; it means every column in the table, which is the six-column result she rejected.
FROM is never optional in a query against a table, because without it the engine has no table to read.
Right - the SELECT list controls which columns appear, and the absence of WHERE leaves all five rows in.
The asterisk is not a wildcard inside a comparison, so this looks for an ITEM_ID stored as a literal asterisk and returns zero rows.
questions.takeaway: The SELECT list decides the columns; leaving out WHERE is what keeps every row.

questions.scenarioTitle: The warehouse manager wants the description first
questions.stem: KimTay's warehouse manager prints a pick list and wants DESCRIPTION on the left, then ITEM_ID, then PRICE. The ITEM table was created with ITEM_ID first. What is true about getting the order he wants?
options: The order of names in the SELECT list is the order the columns appear in the result
Results always come back in the order the columns were declared in the CREATE TABLE statement
The table has to be created again with the columns in the new order to change the output
ORDER BY is the clause that decides which column prints on the left of each row
optionNotes: Right - SELECT DESCRIPTION, ITEM_ID, PRICE FROM ITEM; returns the same five rows with the description on the left.
Declaration order is only the default that SELECT * follows, and naming the columns yourself overrides it.
Nothing about the stored table changes; the SELECT list rearranges the result, not the table.
ORDER BY sorts rows from top to bottom and has no effect on the left-to-right order of columns.
questions.takeaway: Column order in the result comes from your SELECT list, not from how the table was built.

questions.stem: Someone at KimTay wants the customers in Maple Grove and types WHERE CITY = Maple Grove with no quotation marks anywhere. What happens, and why?
options: Text works without quotation marks as long as the value starts with a capital letter
The query returns zero rows quietly, because unquoted text is treated as an empty value
Quotation marks belong only around numbers such as BALANCE, never around words
The statement fails with an error, because unquoted words are read as names rather than as text
optionNotes: Capital letters mean nothing to the parser, and anything left unquoted is read as a name rather than as text.
There is no quiet empty result here, because the statement never runs; the engine rejects it before any row is examined.
It is the other way around: numbers are written bare and character values are wrapped in single quotes.
Right - write WHERE CITY = 'Maple Grove', which returns customers 1120 and 1310. Two bare words break the syntax outright, and a single bare word such as Northfield is reported as an unknown column.
questions.takeaway: Character values go inside single quotes; leave them off and the engine reads your text as a name and refuses to run the statement.

quizzes.heading: Knowledge check: compound conditions and BETWEEN

questions.stem: Against KimTay's ITEM table, WHERE CATEGORY = 'Habitat' OR CATEGORY = 'Food' AND PRICE < 30 returns AV07 and FT88, while WHERE (CATEGORY = 'Habitat' OR CATEGORY = 'Food') AND PRICE < 30 returns FT88 alone. Why do they differ?
options: OR is evaluated first, so the unparenthesized query tested category and price together
AND is evaluated before OR, so without parentheses the price test applied only to Food
The queries are identical; the difference comes from the order rows are stored on disk
Parentheses change which columns are returned, so the second query dropped a row
optionNotes: The precedence runs the other way, which is exactly why the unparenthesized version behaved unexpectedly.
Right - it reads as Habitat OR (Food AND PRICE < 30), so both Habitat rows came back untested on price.
The two results differ by a row, so they cannot be identical, and stored order never changes which rows match.
Parentheses group conditions inside the WHERE clause and have no effect on the SELECT list.
questions.takeaway: AND binds tighter than OR, so add parentheses whenever you mix the two.

questions.stem: KimTay's buyer asks for every item priced from 15.25 through 27.75, endpoints included. A clerk runs WHERE PRICE BETWEEN 15.25 AND 27.75 and gets GR15 at 15.25 and FT88 at 27.75. Which statement describes what BETWEEN did?
options: BETWEEN excluded both endpoints, so only items strictly inside the window came back
BETWEEN worked on whole numbers only, so the engine rounded the prices before comparing
BETWEEN kept the low endpoint but dropped the high one, which is why FT88 is a surprise
BETWEEN includes both endpoints, so items priced exactly 15.25 and exactly 27.75 both match
optionNotes: If both endpoints were excluded, neither GR15 nor FT88 would appear, since each sits exactly on a bound.
No rounding happens; the stored prices are compared against the bounds as written.
FT88 is not a surprise, because the high endpoint is included in the same way the low one is.
Right - BETWEEN 15.25 AND 27.75 means PRICE >= 15.25 AND PRICE <= 27.75.
questions.takeaway: BETWEEN is inclusive at both ends, the same as >= paired with <=.

questions.stem: A student writes WHERE PRICE BETWEEN 27.75 AND 15.25 against KimTay's ITEM table, expecting the same two items as before. The result is empty and no error appears. What went wrong?
options: BETWEEN needs the smaller value first; reversed, the condition can never be true for any row
The engine sorts the two endpoints for you, so an empty result means the data changed
BETWEEN cannot be used on PRICE at all, because that column holds decimal values
The two numbers needed OR between them rather than the keyword AND
optionNotes: Right - it expands to PRICE >= 27.75 AND PRICE <= 15.25, which no single price can satisfy.
No engine reorders your endpoints, so the low bound has to be written first or nothing matches.
BETWEEN works on any comparable type, decimals included, so the column type is not the problem.
The AND inside BETWEEN is part of the operator's syntax, not a joiner you are free to swap for OR.
questions.takeaway: Write BETWEEN low AND high; reversed endpoints return an empty result without complaining.

quizzes.heading: Knowledge check: LIKE patterns and IN lists

questions.scenarioTitle: The streets that end in St.
questions.stem: KimTay is mailing a flyer to customers whose STREET value ends in St. The four stored streets are 215 Foster Ave., 642 Chestnut St., 89 River Rd., and 77 Elm St. Which condition finds the right two?
options: STREET LIKE 'St.' matches any street with those characters somewhere inside the value
STREET LIKE '_St.' matches every street ending in St. no matter how long it is
STREET LIKE '%St.%' is the only pattern that can anchor a match to the end
STREET LIKE '%St.' matches any value ending in St., which is customers 1225 and 1420
optionNotes: With no wildcard at all, LIKE behaves like equals, so this matches only a street stored as exactly St.
The underscore stands for exactly one character, so this matches four-character values such as 1St. and finds nothing here.
A trailing percent sign allows extra characters after St., which unanchors the end rather than anchoring it.
Right - the percent sign stands for any run of characters, and ending the pattern at St. anchors the match.
questions.takeaway: Percent stands for any number of characters, so where you place it decides what gets anchored.

questions.stem: KimTay's item IDs are always four characters: AV07, CF21, DG04, FT88, GR15. The warehouse manager wants the ones whose second character is F. Which condition does that?
options: ITEM_ID LIKE '%F%' does the job, because the percent sign stands for one character
ITEM_ID LIKE '_F__' matches four characters with F in second place, which is CF21 alone
ITEM_ID LIKE 'F___' matches IDs whose second character is F, returning FT88
Underscores are not wildcards, so that pattern matches an ID typed with underscores
optionNotes: Percent stands for any number of characters rather than one, so this finds F anywhere and returns CF21 and FT88.
Right - one underscore, then F, then two underscores pins the F to the second position and matches CF21.
That pattern pins F to the first position, so it returns FT88, whose second character is actually T.
The underscore is the single-character wildcard in LIKE, working alongside the percent sign.
questions.takeaway: Underscore matches exactly one character, so it pins a value to a fixed position and length.

questions.stem: KimTay's bookkeeper wants every customer in Maple Grove or Brookville and writes WHERE CITY = 'Maple Grove' AND CITY = 'Brookville'. The result is empty. What is the fix?
options: The AND version is correct, because a row is allowed to belong to a list of two cities
IN ('Maple Grove', 'Brookville') would drop Brookville, because only the first value in a list counts
One CITY value cannot equal both; use IN ('Maple Grove', 'Brookville'), which returns three customers
Nothing is wrong with AND here; the empty result means the city names are misspelled in the table
optionNotes: AND demands that both conditions be true for the same row, and one stored city cannot be two cities at once.
IN tests the column against every value in the list, so Brookville counts exactly as much as Maple Grove does.
Right - IN is shorthand for the OR chain, and it returns customers 1120, 1310, and 1420.
The stored city names are spelled correctly; the logic is what makes the condition impossible to satisfy.
questions.takeaway: IN matches one column against several values at once, which is what OR does and AND cannot.

matchers.heading: Match each query to the job its operator is doing
matchers.prompt: Eight queries a KimTay analyst wrote in one afternoon. Click a query, then click the job that its `WHERE` clause or `SELECT` list is performing.

zones.label: Range between two values
zones.hint: A low bound and a high bound

cards.text: `SELECT ITEM_ID, PRICE FROM ITEM WHERE PRICE BETWEEN 15.25 AND 27.75;`
cards.why: BETWEEN sets a low and a high bound and includes both, so FT88 and GR15 come back.

cards.text: `SELECT ITEM_ID, PRICE FROM ITEM WHERE PRICE >= 15.25 AND PRICE <= 27.75;`
cards.why: This is the same range written the long way, and it returns the same two rows, FT88 and GR15.

cards.text: `SELECT ITEM_ID, DESCRIPTION FROM ITEM WHERE DESCRIPTION LIKE '%Kit';`
cards.why: The percent sign absorbs everything before Kit, so the two kits FT88 and GR15 match.

cards.text: `SELECT ITEM_ID, DESCRIPTION FROM ITEM WHERE ITEM_ID LIKE '_F__';`
cards.why: The pattern is four positions long with a literal F pinned second, so CF21 matches and nothing else does.

cards.text: `SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CITY FROM CUSTOMER WHERE CITY IN ('Maple Grove', 'Brookville');`
cards.why: IN accepts a row when CITY equals any value in the list, which is customers 1120, 1310, and 1420.

cards.text: `SELECT ITEM_ID, CATEGORY FROM ITEM WHERE CATEGORY IN ('Food', 'Grooming');`
cards.why: Two accepted category values, so CF21 and GR15 qualify and the other three items do not.

cards.text: `SELECT ITEM_ID, ON_HAND * PRICE AS ON_HAND_VALUE FROM ITEM;`
cards.why: No filtering happens at all; all five rows come back with a calculated stock value beside them.

cards.text: `SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CREDIT_LIMIT - BALANCE AS AVAILABLE_CREDIT FROM CUSTOMER;`
cards.why: Subtracting one stored column from another gives all four customers their remaining credit.

matchers.heading: Sort each query by how much of the table it brings back
matchers.prompt: Run these against the KimTay data in your head before you place them. Click a query, then click whether it returns every row of its table, only some rows, or no rows at all.

cards.text: `SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM FROM CUSTOMER WHERE STATE = 'OH';`
cards.why: All four KimTay customers are in Ohio, so a real condition still lets every row through.

cards.text: `SELECT ITEM_ID FROM ITEM WHERE PRICE > 0;`

blocks.text: A query answers a question. The order the answer arrives in decides whether anyone can use it. A list of 200 customers is a wall of text; the same 200 customers alphabetized is a phone directory. That is what `ORDER BY` is for.

blocks.label: Rows have no built-in order
blocks.text: A table is a set of rows, not a list, so there is no such thing as the natural order of a table -- the DBMS hands back rows in whatever order is cheapest for it that day, and that order can change without warning. If you care about the order, you have to ask for it.
4-2a Using the ORDER BY Clause

You have used `ORDER BY` already. Here is the rule behind it: `ORDER BY` is the last clause in a `SELECT` statement, and it names the column you want the output sorted on. That column is called the sort key.
That returns all four KimTay customers, alphabetized by name: Access Pet Center, Companion Care Clinic, Downtown Aquarium & Pets, then Whiskers & Wags Boutique.

blocks.caption: Result of the customer listing sorted by CUSTOMER_NAME

blocks.label: Why the sandbox shows 3512.5
blocks.text: MySQL stores `BALANCE` as `DECIMAL(9,2)` and prints every value with two decimal places, so you see 3512.50 and 0.00; the SQLite engine behind the sandbox on this page drops trailing zeros and prints the same numbers as 3512.5 and 0. Only the display differs -- the stored values, the comparisons, and the sort order are identical, so the tables in this lesson use the MySQL form throughout.

blocks.label: Sort key
blocks.text: A sort key is the column (or expression) whose values decide the order of the rows in the result; sorting rearranges the answer only, and never touches the rows stored in the table.

Sorting runs from low to high unless you say otherwise. That is ascending order, and its keyword is `ASC`. Because ascending is the default, you almost never type `ASC` -- you type `DESC` when you want the largest value on top.

All five items come back most expensive first: AV07 at 64.99, CF21 at 42.50, FT88 at 27.75, GR15 at 15.25, and DG04 at 11.99. Drop the word `DESC` and the same five rows come back in the opposite order, cheapest first.
Text sorts the same way, low to high, which for letters means A to Z. `ORDER BY DESCRIPTION DESC` returns the KimTay items starting at Small Animal Grooming Kit and ending at Aviary Starter Cage.

blocks.label: Capital letters and text order
blocks.text: MySQL's default collation ignores case, so `apple` and `Apple` sort together, while SQLite compares raw character codes, which places every uppercase letter ahead of every lowercase letter; every text value in both case databases begins with a capital letter, so the two engines return the same order for the queries in this lesson.
Where ORDER BY sits

A single-table `SELECT` has a fixed clause order: `SELECT`, then `FROM`, then `WHERE`, then `ORDER BY`. Reading it out loud is a good way to remember what the DBMS does -- it takes the table, throws away the rows that fail the `WHERE` test, and sorts whatever survived.

SELECT ITEM_ID, DESCRIPTION, ON_HAND
FROM ITEM
WHERE ON_HAND > 20
ORDER BY ON_HAND DESC;
Four rows come back -- DG04 with 120, CF21 with 48, FT88 with 30, and GR15 with 22. AV07 has 15 on hand, so it never reaches the sort at all. Filtering happens first, sorting happens to what is left.

blocks.label: ORDER BY goes last
blocks.text: The `WHERE` clause must come before the `ORDER BY` clause; write them the other way around and the DBMS rejects the whole statement with a syntax error instead of guessing what you meant.

blocks.text: 4-2b Additional Sorting Options

One sort key is often not enough. KimTay's route planner wants the customer list arranged by town, and inside each town arranged by name. That takes two sort keys, separated by a comma, listed in order of importance.

Whiskers & Wags Boutique (Brookville) comes first, then the two Maple Grove customers in name order -- Access Pet Center ahead of Companion Care Clinic -- and Downtown Aquarium & Pets (Northfield) last.

blocks.caption: Customers sorted by CITY, then by CUSTOMER_NAME inside each city

blocks.label: Major and minor sort keys
blocks.text: The first column listed is the major sort key and decides the overall order; the second is the minor sort key and is consulted only when two rows tie on the major key -- swap `ORDER BY CITY, CUSTOMER_NAME` for `ORDER BY CITY, BALANCE` and the two Maple Grove rows flip, because Companion Care Clinic's 0.00 now sorts ahead of Access Pet Center's 3512.50.
`DESC` belongs to the one key it follows, not to the whole clause. If you want both keys reversed, you have to write `DESC` twice.

Now the towns run Z to A -- Northfield, Maple Grove, Maple Grove, Brookville -- and inside Maple Grove the larger balance leads, so Access Pet Center at 3512.50 sits above Companion Care Clinic at 0.00.

cards.title: ORDER BY CITY, BALANCE DESC
cards.body: Towns A to Z, and inside a town the largest balance first: Brookville, then Access Pet Center at 3512.50 above Companion Care Clinic at 0.00, then Northfield. Only `BALANCE` is reversed; `CITY` stays ascending because nothing was written after it.

cards.title: ORDER BY CITY DESC, BALANCE DESC
cards.body: Towns Z to A, and inside a town the largest balance first, so Northfield leads and Brookville trails. Each key needed its own `DESC`, which is the mistake people make most often with two sort keys.

blocks.text: Mixed directions are common in real reports. StayWell's leasing office wants one property at a time, priciest room first inside each property.

blocks.caption: Rooms by property, most expensive first within each property

blocks.label: Where NULLs land
blocks.text: Every row shipped with the KimTay and StayWell databases is fully populated, so no result in this lesson contains a NULL, but you will meet them eventually: MySQL and SQLite both place NULL ahead of every non-null value in an ascending sort, while some other systems put NULLs at the end, so check your DBMS before you promise anyone a NULL-safe report.
Sorting on a computed column

You can sort on a value the table does not store. KimTay's bookkeeper wants the items ranked by how much money is sitting on the shelf, which is `ON_HAND` times `PRICE`. Give the calculation a name with `AS`, then sort by that name.

The ranking is CF21 at 2040.00, DG04 at 1438.80, AV07 at 974.85, FT88 at 832.50, and GR15 at 335.50. Note that the cheapest item, the 11.99 leash, is the second most valuable line on the shelf because there are 120 of them -- a ranking you cannot get by sorting on `PRICE` or on `ON_HAND` alone.

blocks.label: Alias or expression
blocks.text: MySQL and SQLite both let `ORDER BY` use the alias you defined in the `SELECT` list, and both also accept the full expression `ORDER BY ON_HAND * PRICE DESC`; repeating the expression is the version that works on every DBMS you are likely to meet, and the same trailing-zero difference applies to the computed column, which MySQL prints as 2040.00 and the sandbox prints as 2040.0.
Sorting by column position
`ORDER BY` also accepts a number, which means the column in that position in the `SELECT` list. `ORDER BY 2` sorts on the second column you selected.

This returns the leash (Accessory), the dry food (Food), the grooming kit (Grooming), then the two Habitat rows with the 64.99 cage ahead of the 27.75 filter kit -- exactly what `ORDER BY CATEGORY, PRICE DESC` returns.

blocks.label: Handy, but brittle
blocks.text: Position numbers break silently: add one column to the `SELECT` list and `ORDER BY 2` quietly starts sorting on something else, so use column names in any script you plan to keep and save the numbers for throwaway queries.

items.title: Decide what the reader scans first
items.body: The column someone's eye runs down is the major sort key -- town for a route sheet, category for a reorder sheet, name for a directory.

items.title: Decide how ties should break
items.body: Add a minor sort key for the rows that share a value in the major key. Two Maple Grove customers need a second key or their order is unpredictable.

items.title: Mark the reversals
items.body: Attach `DESC` to each key that should run high to low. A key with nothing after it stays ascending.

items.title: Put the clause last
items.body: Write `SELECT`, `FROM`, `WHERE`, then `ORDER BY`, and run it. If the order looks wrong, check which key is doing the deciding before you change anything else.

questions.stem: KimTay's warehouse manager wants one printout of the ITEM table with all items of the same category together, and inside each category the most expensive item at the top. Which `ORDER BY` clause does that?
options: `ORDER BY PRICE DESC, CATEGORY` so the price decides the layout and category breaks the ties
`ORDER BY CATEGORY, PRICE DESC` with category as the major key and price descending as the minor key
`ORDER BY CATEGORY DESC, PRICE DESC` so the entire listing reads downward from top to bottom
`ORDER BY CATEGORY, PRICE` because naming both columns puts the higher prices first automatically
optionNotes: Price becomes the major key, so categories are scattered -- the two Habitat rows land in positions 1 and 3, split apart by the Food row -- and `CATEGORY` is never even consulted, because no two items share a price.
Correct: the major key gathers each category together and the descending minor key puts the priciest item of each category on top, so the Habitat block reads 64.99 then 27.75.
The extra `DESC` on `CATEGORY` reverses the category order to Habitat, Grooming, Food, Accessory, which the manager did not ask for.
Sorting defaults to ascending, so this puts the cheapest item of each category first -- the Habitat block would read 27.75 then 64.99, and `DESC` is what flips it.
questions.takeaway: List sort keys in order of importance and attach `DESC` to each key that must run high to low.

questions.stem: StayWell's leasing office needs the rooms that rent for 500.00 or more, cheapest first. Which statement produces exactly that?
options: `SELECT PROPERTY_ID, ROOM_NUM, MONTHLY_RENT FROM ROOM ORDER BY MONTHLY_RENT WHERE MONTHLY_RENT >= 500;`
`SELECT PROPERTY_ID, ROOM_NUM, MONTHLY_RENT FROM ROOM WHERE MONTHLY_RENT >= 500 ORDER BY MONTHLY_RENT DESC;`
`SELECT PROPERTY_ID, ROOM_NUM, MONTHLY_RENT FROM ROOM ORDER BY MONTHLY_RENT;`
`SELECT PROPERTY_ID, ROOM_NUM, MONTHLY_RENT FROM ROOM WHERE MONTHLY_RENT >= 500 ORDER BY MONTHLY_RENT;`
optionNotes: `ORDER BY` has to be the last clause, so putting `WHERE` after it is a syntax error and the statement returns nothing at all.
The filter is right but `DESC` reverses the request: this leads with P200 201 at 725.00 instead of the cheapest qualifying room.
With no `WHERE` clause this returns all five rooms, including P100 102 at 450.00 and P200 202 at 465.00, which do not belong on the report.
Correct: `WHERE` keeps the three rooms at 500.00 or more and the ascending sort returns P100 101 at 595.00, P200 101 at 610.00, then P200 201 at 725.00.
questions.takeaway: The clause order is `SELECT`, `FROM`, `WHERE`, `ORDER BY`, and that is also the order the work happens in.

questions.stem: KimTay's bookkeeper wants the items ranked by the value sitting on the shelf, which is `ON_HAND` multiplied by `PRICE`, largest total first. What should the query do?

Give up on sorting a calculation and store the total in a new column of ITEM first

blocks.text: Every query you have written so far handed back rows: three reps, five items, the customers in Maple Grove. Business questions are often smaller than that. KimTay's owner does not want the five `ITEM` rows on screen. The answer wanted is one number -- how many items are there, what do they average, which one costs the most.

blocks.label: Aggregate function
blocks.text: An aggregate function reads many rows and returns one value. SQL gives you five: `COUNT`, `SUM`, `AVG`, `MAX`, and `MIN`. They are also called set functions, because they work on a whole set of rows instead of one row at a time.

The shape of the statement does not change. You still write `SELECT`, `FROM`, and `WHERE` when you need it. What changes is that the `SELECT` list holds a function call instead of a column name, and the result is a single row no matter how many rows went in.
4-3a Counting rows with COUNT
`COUNT(*)` counts rows. The asterisk stands for the whole row, so nothing inside a row can keep that row from being counted.

SELECT COUNT(*)
FROM ITEM;
One row comes back holding the value 5, because KimTay stocks five items. Notice that the column heading is the function call itself, which is awkward to read on a report.
Name the result with `AS`, the same way you named a computed column in 4-1. A `WHERE` clause still works exactly as it did, because it runs before the counting starts.
That returns one row with `ITEM_COUNT` = 2. `WHERE` keeps the Aviary Starter Cage and the Fish Tank Filter Kit, and `COUNT(*)` counts what survived.
You can also count a named column instead of the whole row, and that is where the two forms part company.

SELECT COUNT(*) AS ALL_ROWS, COUNT(REP_NUM) AS WITH_A_REP
FROM CUSTOMER;

Both columns come back as 4, because every one of the four KimTay customers shipped with the course has a rep number on file. The two forms are not the same thing, though -- they only happen to agree while the data is complete.

cards.title: COUNT(*)
cards.body: Counts rows. Every row that got past the `WHERE` clause adds one, whatever is or is not stored inside it. Use it when the question is "how many records".

cards.title: COUNT(column)
cards.body: Counts values in that one column. Rows where the column is null add nothing. Use it when the question is "how many records have this filled in".

blocks.label: Nulls change the answer
blocks.text: A null is the absence of a value, so `COUNT` on a column steps over it. Nothing in the shipped KimTay data is null, so you have to create one to see it: if KimTay reassigned Companion Care Clinic and left its `REP_NUM` null for a week, `COUNT(*)` would still report 4 while `COUNT(REP_NUM)` reported 3. A staffing report built on the wrong one is off by a customer, and nothing in the output tells you so.

blocks.hint: Both statements run together, and only the SELECT prints a result. Press Reset when you are done -- it reloads the original KimTay data with the rep number back in place.

blocks.text: 4-3b Adding a column up with SUM
`SUM` adds up the values in one numeric column. Ask for the money KimTay is owed across every account.

SELECT SUM(BALANCE) AS TOTAL_OWED
FROM CUSTOMER;
One row comes back with `TOTAL_OWED` = 9533.25, which is 3512.50 plus 1200.00 plus 0.00 plus 4820.75. Add a `WHERE` clause and you total a slice of the table instead.

That returns 3512.5 -- Access Pet Center plus Companion Care Clinic, whose balance is zero. The sandbox drops the trailing zero because SQLite stores the number rather than the display format; MySQL prints 3512.50, since `BALANCE` is declared `DECIMAL(9,2)`. The value is the same either way.

items.title: Start with the table in FROM
items.body: SQL begins with all four rows of `CUSTOMER`. Nothing has been added up yet.

items.title: Drop the rows WHERE rejects
items.body: `WHERE REP_NUM = '20'` leaves two rows standing. This always happens before the function runs.

items.title: Collapse what is left
items.body: `SUM` walks the surviving rows and adds their `BALANCE` values into one number.

items.title: Hand back one row
items.body: The result set has exactly one row and one column, named by your `AS` clause.

blocks.label: An empty result still answers
blocks.text: `SUM` skips nulls the same way `COUNT(column)` does. And when the `WHERE` clause leaves nothing standing, the query still returns one row: `SELECT COUNT(*) AS ROWS_FOUND, SUM(BALANCE) AS TOTAL FROM CUSTOMER WHERE BALANCE > 10000;` reports `ROWS_FOUND` = 0 and an empty `TOTAL`, because `COUNT` of nothing is 0 while `SUM` of nothing is null. SQLite and MySQL behave identically here.
4-3c AVG, MAX, and MIN
These three read a column the same way `SUM` does. `AVG` averages the values, `MAX` returns the largest, `MIN` returns the smallest. You can call several of them in one `SELECT` list.

SELECT AVG(PRICE) AS AVG_PRICE,
       MAX(PRICE) AS HIGHEST,
       MIN(PRICE) AS LOWEST
FROM ITEM;

One row comes back: `AVG_PRICE` = 32.496, `HIGHEST` = 64.99 (the Aviary Starter Cage), `LOWEST` = 11.99 (the Nylon Dog Leash). The average carries more decimal places than any price in the table, which is normal -- an average is a calculated number, not a stored one. One display difference to expect: MySQL widens the scale when it averages a `DECIMAL` column and prints 32.496000, while the SQLite sandbox prints 32.496; the value is the same.

`AVG` divides by the number of values it found, not by the number of rows in the table. On `CUSTOMER`, `SELECT AVG(BALANCE) AS AVG_BALANCE FROM CUSTOMER;` returns 2383.3125 (MySQL writes it as 2383.312500), which is 9533.25 divided by 4. Companion Care Clinic's 0.00 is a real value, so it is counted and it pulls the average down.

blocks.label: Null is not zero
blocks.text: Try this in the 4-3a sandbox, then press Reset to restore the data: run `UPDATE CUSTOMER SET BALANCE = NULL WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '1310';` followed by `SELECT SUM(BALANCE) AS TOTAL, AVG(BALANCE) AS AVG_BALANCE, COUNT(BALANCE) AS COUNTED FROM CUSTOMER;`. The total stays 9533.25, but the average jumps from 2383.3125 to 3177.75 because `COUNTED` is now 3. A zero is a number you divide by; a null is a row the average never sees.
`MAX` and `MIN` are not limited to money. On dates they give you earliest and latest, and on character columns they give you alphabetical order.

That returns 2026-06-14 and 2026-06-15, the two days KimTay billed. Run `SELECT MIN(LAST_NAME) AS FIRST_ALPHABETICALLY, MAX(LAST_NAME) AS LAST_ALPHABETICALLY FROM REP;` and you get Hull and Perez, the ends of the rep list by last name.

blocks.label: Do not mix an aggregate with a plain column yet
blocks.text: `SELECT DESCRIPTION, MAX(PRICE) FROM ITEM;` looks like it should name the costliest item, but one aggregate value cannot line up with five descriptions. SQLite has a special rule for a query whose only aggregate is a lone `MIN` or `MAX`, so it answers Aviary Starter Cage with 64.99, while MySQL rejects the statement under its default `ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY` setting -- the same SQL behaves differently depending on where you run it, which is reason enough not to lean on it. Keep aggregates on their own for now; 4-4 shows the subquery that pairs a value with its row, and 4-5 shows the `GROUP BY` that gives one aggregate per group.
4-3d The DISTINCT operator
Some questions are about variety rather than volume. Ask for the cities KimTay's customers are in and you get one row per customer, not one row per city.

SELECT CITY
FROM CUSTOMER;

Four rows come back, one per customer: Maple Grove, Northfield, Maple Grove, and Brookville. There is no `ORDER BY` here, so the engine may hand them back in any order it likes; what matters is that Maple Grove appears twice, because two customers are there. That is correct as a list of customers and wrong as a list of cities.
Now three rows come back in the order Brookville, Maple Grove, Northfield. `DISTINCT` removed the duplicate before `ORDER BY` sorted what was left.
`DISTINCT` applies to the whole `SELECT` list, not to the column next to it. Two rows have to match on every selected column before one of them is dropped.
That still returns three rows, because the two Maple Grove customers share a state as well as a city. All four KimTay customers are in OH, so `SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT STATE) FROM CUSTOMER;` returns 1.
`DISTINCT` also goes inside `COUNT`, where it changes the question from "how many" to "how many different".

SELECT COUNT(*) AS ALL_ROWS,
       COUNT(CITY) AS CITY_VALUES,
       COUNT(DISTINCT CITY) AS DIFFERENT_CITIES
FROM CUSTOMER;

One row comes back: 4, 4, and 3. The first counts customers, the second counts customers whose city is filled in, the third counts cities. Three different business questions, three different numbers, one table.

SELECT COUNT(*) AS LINE_COUNT,
       COUNT(DISTINCT INVOICE_NUM) AS INVOICES,
       COUNT(DISTINCT ITEM_ID) AS ITEMS
FROM INVOICE_LINE;
That returns 6, 3, and 5. There are six invoice lines spread across three invoices, and they cover five different items because CF21 was ordered on invoice 50710 and again on 50711.

blocks.label: Where DISTINCT goes
blocks.text: `DISTINCT` is an operator, not a function, so it takes no parentheses of its own. On its own it sits immediately after `SELECT` and covers the entire select list. Inside a count it sits inside the parentheses, as in `COUNT(DISTINCT CITY)`. Counting two columns inside one `COUNT` is one of the few places the engines disagree: `COUNT(DISTINCT CITY, STATE)` is an error in the SQLite sandbox but legal in MySQL, where it counts distinct city-and-state pairs. Give one count one column and the statement runs the same way everywhere.

blocks.text: KimTay's warehouse manager wants a list of the items that cost more than the average item. Read that request again and you will notice it is two questions stacked on top of each other: what is the average price across the whole table, and then which rows beat that number? Everything you have written so far answers one question at a time, so this one does not fit into a flat `WHERE` clause.
Here is the statement most people try first.

It does not run. SQLite answers `misuse of aggregate function AVG()` and MySQL answers `Invalid use of group function`. The reason is worth remembering: a `WHERE` clause is tested against one row at a time, and one row has no average. `AVG(PRICE)` is a fact about all five rows together, so it has to be worked out before the row-by-row filtering starts.

blocks.label: Subquery
blocks.text: A subquery is a complete `SELECT` statement written inside parentheses within another statement. The database runs the inner query first, keeps its result, and then runs the outer query using that result as though you had typed the value in yourself.
A subquery that returns one value
Build it in two moves. First write the inner query on its own so you can see what it produces.

SELECT AVG(PRICE)
FROM ITEM;

That returns a single row with a single column. The five prices add up to 162.48, so the answer is 32.496. This page (SQLite) prints `32.496`; MySQL prints `32.496000`, because averaging a `DECIMAL` column widens the number of decimal places it reports. The value is the same either way. One row, one column -- that is exactly what a comparison operator such as `>` or `=` needs on its right-hand side.
Now drop that query, parentheses and all, into the spot where the number would go.

SELECT ITEM_ID, DESCRIPTION, PRICE
FROM ITEM
WHERE PRICE > (SELECT AVG(PRICE) FROM ITEM)
ORDER BY PRICE DESC;

blocks.caption: Result: the two items priced above the 32.496 average

blocks.label: Trailing zeros on screen
blocks.text: The tables in this lesson print prices the way the data was entered, so CF21 shows as `42.50`. SQLite does not pad numbers to a fixed number of decimal places, so the sandbox on this page will show `42.5` for the same value; MySQL, which stores the column as `DECIMAL(7,2)`, shows `42.50`. Same number, different display -- do not treat it as a wrong answer.

Trace the order of events. The inner query runs once and produces 32.496. The outer query then behaves exactly as if you had written `WHERE PRICE > 32.496`. The difference is that nobody had to work the average out by hand, so the statement stays correct tomorrow when prices change.

blocks.label: Three habits that prevent errors
blocks.text: Wrap the subquery in parentheses, select exactly one column inside it, and put no semicolon inside the parentheses -- the semicolon belongs at the very end of the whole statement.
When = is safe

A comparison with `=` is safe whenever the subquery cannot possibly return more than one row. Suppose a buyer wants every item that shares a category with item `FT88`. You do not have to know that the category is Habitat; you can look it up.

That returns one row holding `Habitat`. It can never return two, because `ITEM_ID` is the primary key of `ITEM` and a primary key value matches at most one row. That guarantee is what makes `=` legitimate in the outer query.

SELECT ITEM_ID, DESCRIPTION, PRICE
FROM ITEM
WHERE CATEGORY = (SELECT CATEGORY FROM ITEM WHERE ITEM_ID = 'FT88')
ORDER BY ITEM_ID;

blocks.caption: Result: both Habitat items, including FT88 itself

blocks.label: FT88 matches itself
blocks.text: `FT88` appears in its own result because its category equals its own category; if the buyer wants the other Habitat items, add `AND ITEM_ID <> 'FT88'` to the outer `WHERE` clause.

blocks.solution:
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, BALANCE
FROM CUSTOMER
WHERE BALANCE > (SELECT AVG(BALANCE) FROM CUSTOMER)
ORDER BY BALANCE DESC;
blocks.hint: Run it to see all four customers, then add a WHERE that compares BALANCE to a subquery over the whole table -- the four balances total 9533.25, so the average is 2383.3125 and two customers should survive.

blocks.text: A subquery that returns several values

KimTay's bookkeeper now wants the stock picture for every item that a customer ordered two or more of on any invoice line. The list of qualifying item IDs lives in `INVOICE_LINE`, and the stock figures live in `ITEM`. Start, as always, with the inner query.

Four rows come back: `CF21`, `DG04`, `CF21` and `FT88`. Without an `ORDER BY` the engine may list them in any order, so read the set rather than the sequence. Notice `CF21` appears twice, because it was ordered in quantity on two different invoices. That duplication does not matter here -- asking whether a value is in a list gives the same answer whether the list mentions it once or twice.

A single value would fit next to `=`, but four values will not. `IN` is the operator that compares one value against a whole list, and it accepts a subquery in place of the parenthesised list you met in lesson 4-1h.

SELECT ITEM_ID, DESCRIPTION, ON_HAND
FROM ITEM
WHERE ITEM_ID IN (SELECT ITEM_ID FROM INVOICE_LINE WHERE NUM_ORDERED >= 2)
ORDER BY ITEM_ID;

blocks.caption: Result: the three distinct items ordered two or more at a time

blocks.text: Read the condition out loud as a membership test: keep this `ITEM` row if its `ITEM_ID` is one of the IDs the inner query found. `AV07` and `GR15` were each ordered one at a time, so neither one is in the list and neither one appears.
The classic error: = against many rows
Sooner or later you will write the previous query with `=` instead of `IN`, because the shape of the statement looks identical.

blocks.label: This is where the two engines part ways
blocks.text: MySQL refuses the statement with error 1242, `Subquery returns more than 1 row`. SQLite, the engine running in this page, does not complain at all -- it keeps whichever value the inner query handed back first and returns that single row, which on this data is `CF21`. Nothing promises it will always be `CF21`, because the inner query has no `ORDER BY`; that is the point. A wrong answer delivered with no error message is worse than an error, so treat a silent one-row result from a `=` subquery as a bug to investigate, not as a pass.

cards.title: Reach for =
cards.body: The inner query is an aggregate over the whole table, such as `SELECT AVG(PRICE) FROM ITEM`, or it filters on a primary key, such as `WHERE ITEM_ID = 'FT88'`. In both cases one row is guaranteed.

cards.title: Reach for IN
cards.body: The inner query filters on any non-key column, such as `WHERE NUM_ORDERED >= 2` or `WHERE CITY = 'Maple Grove'`. Today it might return one row by luck; next week's data can return five.

items.title: Write the inner query alone and run it
items.body: You need to see two things before going further: how many rows it returns and how many columns. A subquery used with `=` or `IN` must return exactly one column, or both engines reject the whole statement.

items.title: Count the rows, then pick the operator
items.body: One row that can never become two means `=` (or `>`, `<`, `>=`, `<=`). Any chance of more than one row means `IN`.

items.title: Paste it into the outer query inside parentheses
items.body: Drop the trailing semicolon from the inner query, wrap it in parentheses, and put it where a literal value would otherwise sit.

items.title: Sanity-check the row count
items.body: If the outer query returns exactly one row and you expected several, suspect that you used `=` where `IN` was needed.

SELECT PROPERTY_ID, PROPERTY_NAME
FROM PROPERTY
WHERE PROPERTY_ID IN (SELECT PROPERTY_ID FROM ROOM WHERE ROOM_TYPE = 'Double')
ORDER BY PROPERTY_ID;
blocks.hint: The inner query returns two property IDs, P100 and P200, because each property has one Double room. Nest it inside a query on PROPERTY to name both buildings, then swap IN for = and watch this engine hand back Millbrook Commons on its own.

questions.stem: The warehouse manager wants every row of `ITEM` whose `PRICE` is higher than the average price of all five items, and wants the same saved statement to still be correct after prices change. Which approach meets both requirements?
options: Add `WHERE PRICE > AVG(PRICE)` to a query over the `ITEM` table
Run `SELECT AVG(PRICE) FROM ITEM;`, read 32.496 off the screen, and save `WHERE PRICE > 32.496`
Compare `PRICE` to `(SELECT AVG(PRICE) FROM ITEM)` inside the `WHERE` clause
Write `WHERE PRICE IN (SELECT AVG(PRICE) FROM ITEM)` to match the average
optionNotes: An aggregate cannot appear in `WHERE`, which is tested one row at a time, so SQLite reports misuse of aggregate function and MySQL reports invalid use of group function.
This lists AV07 and CF21 correctly today, but 32.496 is frozen into the text of the statement, so the saved query reports the wrong rows the moment any price changes.
The inner query returns the single value 32.496 first, and the outer query then keeps AV07 at 64.99 and CF21 at 42.50, recomputing the average every time it runs.
`IN` tests for an exact match against the list, and no item is priced at exactly 32.496, so this returns zero rows.
questions.takeaway: Comparing a row to a summary of the whole table requires a subquery, because the summary has to be computed before row-by-row filtering begins -- and computing it inside the statement keeps the statement correct as data changes.

questions.stem: The leasing office runs `SELECT PROPERTY_ID FROM ROOM WHERE ROOM_TYPE = 'Double';` and gets P100 and P200. Someone then nests it in a query on `PROPERTY` using `WHERE PROPERTY_ID = (...)` instead of `IN`. What happens?
options: MySQL rejects it as returning more than one row, while SQLite quietly returns only Millbrook Commons
Both engines return Millbrook Commons and Sycamore Court, because `=` expands into `IN` automatically
The statement returns zero rows, because `=` cannot compare two `CHAR` columns to each other
The subquery is ignored and both StayWell properties come back unfiltered
optionNotes: MySQL raises error 1242, subquery returns more than 1 row; SQLite keeps only the first value the inner query produced, here P100, and reports Millbrook Commons alone with no warning.
`=` never expands into `IN`; a comparison operator demands a single value on its right-hand side and has no way to test membership in a list.
`=` compares `CHAR` values without difficulty, which is why the SQLite result is a plausible-looking single row rather than an empty one.
A subquery is never ignored; it is evaluated before the outer query and its result is always used.
questions.takeaway: A silent single-row answer from a `=` subquery is a warning sign, because the engine may be discarding values instead of reporting the mistake.

questions.stem: A KimTay buyer writes `WHERE CATEGORY = (SELECT CATEGORY FROM ITEM WHERE ITEM_ID = 'FT88')` and gets AV07 and FT88. Why is `=` the correct operator in this statement?
options: `CATEGORY` is unique across `ITEM`, so only one category value can ever exist
`=` always takes the first row whenever a subquery happens to return several
The subquery contains no aggregate function, so it can only ever return one row
`ITEM_ID` is the primary key, so that condition matches at most one row
optionNotes: `CATEGORY` is not unique at all -- AV07 and FT88 share the value Habitat, which is precisely why the outer query returns two rows.
MySQL raises an error rather than taking the first row, so relying on that behaviour produces a statement that fails on the engine used in Module 3.
Plenty of subqueries without aggregates return many rows, such as the `INVOICE_LINE` lookup that returned four item IDs.
A primary key value identifies at most one row, so the inner query is guaranteed to yield the single value Habitat.
questions.takeaway: Choose between `=` and `IN` by asking what guarantees the inner query's row count, not by looking at today's data.
