blocks.text: Lesson 4-3 handed you one number for a whole table: `COUNT(*)` over every item, `AVG(PRICE)` over every price. That is useful about once. What a business actually asks for is the same number broken out by something: the average price per category, the number of customers per rep, the total per invoice. You do not want one answer, you want one answer per pile.

`GROUP BY` builds the piles. It takes the rows that made it past `WHERE`, sorts them into groups that share the same value in the column you name, and runs your aggregate function once inside each group. Then `HAVING` throws away whole groups you do not want. Everything in this lesson still happens inside a single table.

blocks.label: GROUP BY
blocks.text: `GROUP BY column` collapses the rows into one result row per distinct value of that column. Five `ITEM` rows spread across four categories come back as four rows. Any aggregate in the `SELECT` list is then computed separately for each group instead of once for the table.
One row per group

KimTay's warehouse manager wants to know how the catalog is spread across categories and what a typical item costs in each one. The `ITEM` table holds five rows and four category values, so the answer should be four lines long:

blocks.caption: Four rows back, one per CATEGORY

blocks.text: Read `COUNT(*)` differently than you did in Lesson 4-3. It is no longer counting rows in the table, it is counting rows in a group. Habitat is the only category holding more than one item, so it is the only row where the count is 2 and the only row where the average is doing real work: 64.99 for the Aviary Starter Cage and 27.75 for the Fish Tank Filter Kit average out to 46.37. The other three groups hold a single item each, so their average is that item's price.

blocks.label: Two things the output will not do for you
blocks.text: The sandbox prints `42.5` where a MySQL server would print `42.50`. That is an engine difference rather than a different number: the sandbox runs SQLite, which keeps a price as a plain number and drops a trailing zero, while MySQL's `DECIMAL(7,2)` column pads every value it returns out to two decimal places. Expect averages in particular to come back with a different number of decimal places on the two engines. Separately, although SQLite and MySQL both tend to hand grouped rows back in group order, neither one promises to, so if the order matters put an `ORDER BY` on the end exactly as you did in Lesson 4-2.
The grouping column does not have to be a category name. `INVOICE_LINE` stores one row per item on an invoice, so grouping it by `INVOICE_NUM` turns six line rows into a total per invoice:

SELECT INVOICE_NUM, SUM(NUM_ORDERED * QUOTED_PRICE) AS INVOICE_TOTAL
FROM INVOICE_LINE
GROUP BY INVOICE_NUM
ORDER BY INVOICE_TOTAL DESC;

blocks.caption: Six line rows become three invoice totals

blocks.starter:
-- One row per category, with a count:
SELECT CATEGORY, COUNT(*) AS ITEM_COUNT
FROM ITEM
GROUP BY CATEGORY;

-- Your turn: keep the count, add the cheapest and the dearest price
-- in each category, and sort so the biggest category comes first.
blocks.solution:
SELECT CATEGORY, COUNT(*) AS ITEM_COUNT, MIN(PRICE) AS LOWEST, MAX(PRICE) AS HIGHEST
FROM ITEM
GROUP BY CATEGORY
ORDER BY ITEM_COUNT DESC, CATEGORY;
blocks.hint: MIN and MAX group the same way COUNT does. Expect Habitat first with 2, 27.75 and 64.99, then the three single-item categories, where the lowest and the highest are the same price.

blocks.text: The rule: grouped or aggregated, nothing else

Here is the one rule that catches everybody. Every column in the `SELECT` list of a grouped query must either appear in the `GROUP BY` clause or sit inside an aggregate function. There is no third option, and the reason is arithmetic rather than pedantry: the result has one row per group, so every column has to have exactly one value per group.
Watch it break. Someone wants the category counts and thinks adding the product name would be a nice touch:
The Habitat group holds two rows with two different descriptions, and the query has asked for one description. There is no correct answer to give.

blocks.label: This is where the two engines part company
blocks.text: MySQL rejects the statement outright, because its default `ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY` setting refuses a column that is neither grouped nor aggregated. SQLite runs it and quietly picks one row's description out of each group. In this sandbox you get four rows, and the Habitat line carries just one of its two descriptions with no sign that the other item was ever there. Nothing in the SQL decides which one you get, so do not learn the answer this sandbox happens to give. Silent is worse than an error: learn the rule rather than trusting the engine to enforce it.

There are two honest fixes, and picking between them means deciding what question you are asking. Drop `DESCRIPTION` from the `SELECT` list if you want a summary. Add it to `GROUP BY` if you want a finer grain, which changes the question from "per category" to "per category and description" and gives you five rows instead of four:

SELECT CATEGORY, DESCRIPTION, COUNT(*) AS ITEM_COUNT
FROM ITEM
GROUP BY CATEGORY, DESCRIPTION
ORDER BY CATEGORY, DESCRIPTION;
Grouping on more than one column

Listing two columns after `GROUP BY` makes a group out of each distinct combination of the two, not two separate sets of groups. Grouping KimTay's customers by rep and city answers "which rep covers which town, and with how many accounts":

SELECT REP_NUM, CITY, COUNT(*) AS CUSTOMER_COUNT
FROM CUSTOMER
GROUP BY REP_NUM, CITY
ORDER BY REP_NUM, CITY;

blocks.caption: Three combinations exist in the data, so three rows come back

blocks.text: Rep 20 gets one row rather than two because both of that rep's customers, Access Pet Center and Companion Care Clinic, sit in Maple Grove. If one of them moved to Northfield, the same query would return four rows the next time it ran. The number of groups follows the data, never the number of columns you listed.
HAVING: a WHERE clause for groups

Grouping tends to raise a follow-up question, and the follow-up is almost always about the groups themselves. Which categories hold more than one item? Which reps are carrying more than 2,000 dollars of customer balance? Those are tests on a finished group, and the clause that runs them is `HAVING`.

SELECT CATEGORY, COUNT(*) AS ITEM_COUNT
FROM ITEM
GROUP BY CATEGORY
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

blocks.caption: One row survives: only Habitat holds more than one item

blocks.text: Without the `HAVING` line that query returns four rows. With it, the three single-item groups are formed, counted, tested and thrown out. They were built and then discarded, which is exactly what `HAVING` means: the groups all get made, and then some of them do not make the cut.

blocks.label: An aggregate cannot go in WHERE
blocks.text: Moving the same test up to `WHERE COUNT(*) > 1` fails on both engines, because when `WHERE` runs there are no groups yet and so no count to compare against. SQLite reports `misuse of aggregate: COUNT()` and MySQL reports `Invalid use of group function`. Different wording, same reason.
WHERE first, then GROUP BY, then HAVING
You write a query in one order and the engine runs it in another. Committing the running order to memory is what makes the rest of this lesson obvious instead of fiddly.

items.title: 1. FROM picks the table
items.body: All five `ITEM` rows, or all four `CUSTOMER` rows, are on the table to start with.

items.title: 2. WHERE filters rows
items.body: Each row is tested on its own values and either survives or is dropped. Nothing has been grouped or counted yet, which is why an aggregate is illegal here.

items.title: 3. GROUP BY builds the groups
items.body: Only the surviving rows get sorted into piles. A row thrown out in step 2 cannot influence any group's count, sum or average.

items.title: 4. HAVING filters groups
items.body: Every aggregate is now computed, so a test on `COUNT(*)`, `SUM(BALANCE)` or `AVG(PRICE)` finally has something to compare. Whole groups are kept or discarded.

items.title: 5. SELECT produces the output row
items.body: One row per surviving group, holding the grouping columns and the aggregate values.

items.title: 6. ORDER BY sorts the result
items.body: Sorting happens last, on the summary rows, which is why you can order by an aggregate or by a column alias here.

blocks.label: Say it out loud once
blocks.text: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY. Filter rows, build groups, filter groups, report, sort. Almost every confusing result in this lesson is a step that ran earlier or later than you pictured.
When swapping WHERE and HAVING changes the answer
KimTay's bookkeeper has two questions that sound alike in English. Rep 20 has two customers: Access Pet Center with a balance of 3512.50, and Companion Care Clinic with a balance of 0.00.

cards.title: Question A: per rep, how many customers owe more than 1,000?
cards.body: This is a question about customers. Test each customer row for a balance over 1000.00, drop the ones that fail, and count what is left in each rep's pile. The test happens before the grouping, so it belongs in `WHERE`.

cards.title: Question B: which reps' books total more than 1,000, and how many customers do they have?
cards.body: This is a question about reps. Keep every customer row, add up each rep's balances, and drop the reps whose total falls short. The test needs a `SUM` that does not exist until the group is built, so it belongs in `HAVING`.

blocks.text: Same table, same grouping column, same threshold of 1000.00. Here is question A:

SELECT REP_NUM, COUNT(*) AS CUSTOMER_COUNT
FROM CUSTOMER
WHERE BALANCE > 1000.00
GROUP BY REP_NUM
ORDER BY REP_NUM;

blocks.caption: Question A: Companion Care Clinic is dropped before counting

blocks.text: And here is question B, with the identical threshold moved into `HAVING` and applied to a sum:

SELECT REP_NUM, COUNT(*) AS CUSTOMER_COUNT
FROM CUSTOMER
GROUP BY REP_NUM
HAVING SUM(BALANCE) > 1000.00
ORDER BY REP_NUM;

blocks.caption: Question B: nothing is dropped before counting, so rep 20 counts both customers

blocks.text: Look at rep 20: 1 in the first result, 2 in the second. Nothing about the data changed. In query A, Companion Care Clinic's 0.00 balance failed the row test in step 2, so it was gone before `COUNT(*)` ever saw it. In query B no row was filtered at all; rep 20's group was built from both customers, its total came to 3512.50, that total cleared 1000.00, and both rows stayed counted. Neither answer is wrong. They answer different questions, and the clause you put the test in is what picks the question.

blocks.label: A WHERE that empties a group deletes the group
blocks.text: `SELECT CATEGORY, COUNT(*) AS ITEM_COUNT FROM ITEM WHERE PRICE > 20.00 GROUP BY CATEGORY ORDER BY CATEGORY;` returns two rows, Food with 1 and Habitat with 2. Accessory and Grooming do not come back with a count of 0; they do not come back at all, because both of their rows were removed in step 2 and a group is only built from rows that survive. `GROUP BY` can never report on rows that `WHERE` already threw away.

The two clauses are not rivals. Most real reporting queries use both, and reading one of these from top to bottom is reading the pipeline in order: filter the rows, group what is left, filter the groups, sort the survivors.

SELECT REP_NUM, COUNT(*) AS CUSTOMER_COUNT, SUM(BALANCE) AS TOTAL_OWED
FROM CUSTOMER
WHERE BALANCE > 1000.00
GROUP BY REP_NUM
HAVING SUM(BALANCE) > 2000.00
ORDER BY TOTAL_OWED DESC;

blocks.caption: Rep 35 is built as a group, then dropped by HAVING because 1200.00 falls short of 2000.00

blocks.label: A test on the grouping column can sit in either clause
blocks.text: When a query says `GROUP BY CATEGORY`, both `WHERE CATEGORY = 'Habitat'` and `HAVING CATEGORY = 'Habitat'` are legal on either engine and both return the single row `Habitat | 2`, because the grouping column has exactly one value per group. Prefer `WHERE`: it discards the rows before any group is built, so the engine does less work and a reader can tell at a glance that the test is about rows.
Your turn, at StayWell
StayWell's rental office wants a report on the higher-end rooms. Build it one clause at a time and run it after each change, so you can see which step removed what.

blocks.starter:
-- Every property, every room:
SELECT PROPERTY_ID, COUNT(*) AS ROOM_COUNT, AVG(MONTHLY_RENT) AS AVG_RENT
FROM ROOM
GROUP BY PROPERTY_ID
ORDER BY PROPERTY_ID;

-- Your turn, one clause at a time:
--   1. count only rooms renting for more than 500.00
--   2. keep only the properties that still have more than one such room
--   3. sort by average rent, highest first
blocks.solution:
SELECT PROPERTY_ID, COUNT(*) AS ROOM_COUNT, AVG(MONTHLY_RENT) AS AVG_RENT
FROM ROOM
WHERE MONTHLY_RENT > 500.00
GROUP BY PROPERTY_ID
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY AVG_RENT DESC;
blocks.hint: The rent test is about one room row, the count test is about a finished group. The starter gives P100 with 2 rooms at 522.5 and P200 with 3 at 600; the finished query gives one row, P200 with 2 rooms at 667.5.

blocks.text: Run it in stages and the pipeline is visible. Adding `WHERE MONTHLY_RENT > 500.00` drops the 450.00 double at Millbrook Commons and the 465.00 double at Sycamore Court, which pulls P100 down to one room and P200 down to two, and pushes both averages up. Adding `HAVING COUNT(*) > 1` then removes P100 entirely, because after the row filter it has only one qualifying room left.
Checklist for a grouped query

items: Decide what one output row represents. That noun is your `GROUP BY` column list.
Check every entry in the `SELECT` list: it is either in `GROUP BY` or inside an aggregate, with no exceptions.
Put a test that reads one row's own values in `WHERE`, where it will run before any group exists.
Put a test that reads `COUNT`, `SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN` or `MAX` in `HAVING`, where the aggregate is already computed.
Remember that a group whose rows were all removed by `WHERE` does not show up as a zero; it does not show up at all.
Add `ORDER BY` if the order of the summary rows matters, because grouping does not guarantee one.

blocks.label: Naming the aggregate pays off twice
blocks.text: `SUM(BALANCE) AS TOTAL_OWED` gives the column a readable heading and gives `ORDER BY TOTAL_OWED DESC` something short to sort by. Strict standard SQL does not allow that alias back in `HAVING`, but SQLite and MySQL both accept `HAVING TOTAL_OWED > 2000.00`; repeating the full `SUM(BALANCE)` in `HAVING` works everywhere, so that is the safer habit while you are learning.

quizzes.heading: Check yourself: grouping, HAVING, and the order things run

questions.stem: KimTay's warehouse manager asks for a sheet showing how many items are stocked in each product category. The `ITEM` table holds five rows spread across four categories: Accessory, Food, Grooming and Habitat. Someone runs `SELECT CATEGORY, COUNT(*) AS ITEM_COUNT FROM ITEM GROUP BY CATEGORY;`. How many rows come back, and why?
options: Five rows, because `GROUP BY` returns every row of `ITEM` with its category attached to it
One row, because `COUNT(*)` always collapses the whole table down to a single number
Four rows, one per distinct category, each carrying the count of items in that category
Two rows, because only the categories holding more than one item survive the grouping
optionNotes: `GROUP BY` replaces the detail rows with one summary row per group, so the five item rows never appear individually.
`COUNT(*)` collapses to a single number only when there is no `GROUP BY`; here it is computed once inside each group.
Correct -- four distinct category values means four groups, and the Habitat row shows 2 while the other three show 1.
Nothing is filtered here, and a group of one still produces a row; dropping those would take `HAVING COUNT(*) > 1`.
questions.takeaway: `GROUP BY` gives you one result row per distinct group, not one row per underlying table row.

questions.scenarioTitle: The extra column that looked harmless
questions.stem: A student wants the category counts plus the product name, so they write `SELECT CATEGORY, DESCRIPTION, COUNT(*) FROM ITEM GROUP BY CATEGORY;`. The Habitat category holds two items, the Aviary Starter Cage and the Fish Tank Filter Kit. What is wrong with that statement?
options: `DESCRIPTION` is neither named in `GROUP BY` nor wrapped in an aggregate, so the Habitat group has two descriptions and only one slot to report them in
`COUNT(*)` cannot appear beside a text column, so the count has to come out of the select list
Nothing is wrong, because SQL prints every description belonging to a group on its own output line
The statement needs `HAVING DESCRIPTION IS NOT NULL` added before either engine will accept it
optionNotes: Correct -- the Habitat group holds two different descriptions but the result has room for one, so MySQL rejects the statement outright while SQLite runs it and silently reports only one of them.
Counts and text columns mix freely; the real problem is that `DESCRIPTION` varies inside a group while `COUNT(*)` does not.
One row per group is the whole point of `GROUP BY`, so a second Habitat line is exactly what you do not get.
Every description in `ITEM` has a value, and `HAVING` filters finished groups rather than repairing an ungrouped column.
questions.takeaway: Every column in the `SELECT` list must be named in `GROUP BY` or wrapped in an aggregate function.

questions.stem: Rep 20 has two customers: Access Pet Center with a balance of 3512.50 and Companion Care Clinic with a balance of 0.00. Query A is `SELECT REP_NUM, COUNT(*) FROM CUSTOMER WHERE BALANCE > 1000.00 GROUP BY REP_NUM;` and query B is `SELECT REP_NUM, COUNT(*) FROM CUSTOMER GROUP BY REP_NUM HAVING SUM(BALANCE) > 1000.00;`. What does each report for rep 20?
options: Both report 2, because rep 20 has two customers no matter which clause holds the test
Both report 1, because a filter always removes Companion Care Clinic before anything gets counted
A reports 2 and B reports 1, because `HAVING` runs first and discards the zero balance row
A reports 1 and B reports 2, because A drops the zero-balance row before the counting happens
optionNotes: Query A tests each row before grouping, so Companion Care Clinic is already gone by the time `COUNT(*)` runs.
Query B filters no rows at all; it tests the finished group, whose total of 3512.50 clears 1000.00, so both customers stay counted.
`HAVING` runs after the groups are built, not before, so it cannot remove one customer row from inside a group.
Correct -- `WHERE` filters rows first so A counts 1, while `HAVING` tests the group total 3512.50 and keeps both rows, so B counts 2.
questions.takeaway: Moving a threshold from `WHERE` to `HAVING` can change the numbers, because one filters rows and the other filters groups.

questions.stem: StayWell's rental office wants each property's average rent counting only rooms that rent for more than 500.00, and wants to see only the properties left holding more than one such room. Which clause takes which test?
options: Put both tests in `WHERE`, since every filter in SQL belongs in the same clause
`MONTHLY_RENT > 500.00` belongs in `WHERE`, and `COUNT(*) > 1` belongs in `HAVING` after grouping
`MONTHLY_RENT > 500.00` belongs in `HAVING`, and `COUNT(*) > 1` belongs in `WHERE` before grouping
Put both tests in `HAVING`, because the report is a grouped summary rather than a listing of rows
optionNotes: No count exists yet while `WHERE` is running, and both engines reject an aggregate in that clause outright.
Correct -- the rent test reads one room row so it filters first, and the count test reads a finished group so it filters after.
That is backwards: rent is a value on a single room row, while a count only exists once rows have been gathered into groups.

`COUNT(*) > 1` is fine in `HAVING`, but `MONTHLY_RENT` is not. MySQL rejects it there, and this sandbox's SQLite runs it and hands back P100 with 2 rooms at 522.5 and P200 with 3 at 600 -- the rent test removed nothing, so the cheap rooms are still counted and still pulling the averages down.
questions.takeaway: Row-level tests belong in `WHERE`; tests on an aggregate belong in `HAVING`.

matchers.heading: Sort each test into the clause that can run it
matchers.prompt: Each card is a condition from a single-table KimTay query that groups rows. Assume `GROUP BY CATEGORY` for the `ITEM` conditions and `GROUP BY REP_NUM` for the `CUSTOMER` conditions, then drop each card on the clause where it belongs.

cards.why: `PRICE` is a value carried by one item row and is not the grouping column, so the test runs before any group exists.

cards.text: `BALANCE > 1000.00`
cards.why: Each customer row carries its own balance, so this test can be settled row by row before the rows are gathered into rep groups.

cards.text: `ON_HAND > REORDER_LEVEL`
cards.why: Both columns sit on the same item row, so nothing has to be grouped before the comparison can be made.

cards.text: `AVG(PRICE) > 20.00`
cards.why: An average does not exist until a group is complete, and both engines reject an aggregate inside `WHERE`.

cards.text: `COUNT(*) > 1`
cards.why: There is no count until the rows have been piled into groups, so the test can only run after `GROUP BY`.

cards.text: `SUM(BALANCE) > 2000.00`
cards.why: The total across a rep's customers is a group-level number, which makes it a `HAVING` test rather than a row test.

cards.text: `CATEGORY = 'Habitat'`
cards.why: `CATEGORY` is the grouping column and has exactly one value per group, so both clauses accept it on both engines, though `WHERE` discards the rows earlier.
`REP_NUM` is the grouping column, so either clause is legal; put it in `WHERE` so the engine never builds the groups you are about to throw away.

blocks.text: Module 3 introduced the null while you were building tables: a column declared without `NOT NULL` is allowed to hold no value at all, and the data-type lesson already warned you that `WHERE STREET = NULL` never matches anything. This lesson is where that warning stops being a footnote. You will create a null on purpose and watch it change the answers to ordinary queries -- filters, arithmetic, counts and averages -- without ever raising an error.

blocks.label: Null
blocks.text: A null is the absence of a value. It is not zero, it is not an empty string, and it is not the word "unknown" typed into the column. It means the database has nothing recorded in that spot and cannot tell you what belongs there.

StayWell has two columns where a null is the honest answer, and Module 3 declared both of them without `NOT NULL`: `STUDENT.HOME_STATE` and `ROOM.MONTHLY_RENT`. A housing application can arrive with the home state left blank, and a room that is being reconfigured can sit in the ROOM table before anyone has decided next year's rent. In both cases the row exists and the value does not.

Every row that ships with this course is filled in -- there is not a single null anywhere in KimTay or StayWell -- so nothing you have queried so far has contained one. To study how nulls behave you will create one on purpose in your own copy of the data.
Create a null to work with

Suppose StayWell's housing office finds that the home state on one student record was entered from an unreadable form, and clears it until the student confirms it. That is an `UPDATE`, which you learned in Module 3. Run the update, then list the table.

Four rows come back: S001 Nguyen OH, S002 Carter PA, S003 Ibrahim, and S004 Park OH. In the S003 row the HOME_STATE cell reads `NULL`, which is how this page's result grid prints a missing value. Other tools pick other conventions -- some show an empty cell, some print (null) -- and all of them mean the same thing. None of them is a value you can compare against.

blocks.label: This only changes your copy
blocks.text: The database on this page lives in your browser. The update above edits your session and nothing else, and reloading the page or pressing Reset restores the original StayWell rows.
Why = NULL never works
Your first instinct is to look for the missing value with `WHERE HOME_STATE = NULL`. It reads like English and it fails every time. Here is what the database actually does with it.

items.title: Take one row at a time
items.body: The engine walks through STUDENT row by row and asks whether that row's HOME_STATE equals NULL.

items.title: Compare a value against an unknown
items.body: NULL is not a value, it is the absence of one. Asking whether something equals an unknown does not give true or false, it gives a third answer: unknown.

items.title: Keep only what tests true
items.body: WHERE keeps a row only when the condition comes back true. Unknown is not true, so the row is discarded. Every row is discarded, including the one you were hunting for.

blocks.text: That query matches nothing, even though S003 is sitting right there with no home state recorded. Watch what the sandbox prints when you run it underneath the `UPDATE`: instead of an empty grid you get the message `Statement ran. 1 row affected.` That 1 is the update's row, not a match -- the giveaway is that no result table appeared at all. Writing `WHERE HOME_STATE <> NULL` matches nothing for exactly the same reason.

blocks.label: A silent wrong answer
blocks.text: `= NULL` is legal SQL. There is no error, no warning, and no red text -- only an empty result that looks like a truthful "nothing matched." This is one of the easiest ways to hand someone a report that is quietly wrong.
IS NULL and IS NOT NULL

SQL gives you a separate test for the question "is there a value here at all?" It is `IS NULL`, and its opposite is `IS NOT NULL`. Neither one is a comparison, so neither one falls into the unknown trap.
One row comes back -- S003 Ibrahim -- and this time you get a real result grid, with `NULL` printed in the HOME_STATE cell. Flip the test to find the rows that do have a value.

SELECT STUDENT_ID, LAST_NAME, HOME_STATE
FROM STUDENT
WHERE HOME_STATE IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY STUDENT_ID;
Three rows come back: S001 Nguyen OH, S002 Carter PA, and S004 Park OH. One row plus three rows accounts for all four students, which is what you want from a pair of opposite tests.

blocks.caption: Four ways to write a null test, and what each one really does
rows: Is this value equal to an unknown? Answer: unknown
Is this value different from an unknown? Answer: unknown
Is this column empty? Answer: true or false
Does this column hold a value? Answer: true or false

blocks.label: Both engines agree here
blocks.text: `IS NULL` and `IS NOT NULL` work the same way in MySQL and in the SQLite engine running on this page. Each product also offers a shorthand of its own -- MySQL has `<=>` and SQLite has `IS` -- but `IS NULL` is the portable form, so write that one.
Nulls in arithmetic
Room 202 at Sycamore Court is being reconfigured, and next year's rent has not been set. Clear that rent, then price out a nine-month academic year for every room at that property.

UPDATE ROOM
SET MONTHLY_RENT = NULL
WHERE PROPERTY_ID = 'P200' AND ROOM_NUM = '202';

SELECT PROPERTY_ID, ROOM_NUM, MONTHLY_RENT, MONTHLY_RENT * 9 AS NINE_MONTH_TOTAL
FROM ROOM
WHERE PROPERTY_ID = 'P200'
ORDER BY ROOM_NUM;

Three rows come back. Room 101 shows 610 and 5490, room 201 shows 725 and 6525, and room 202 shows `NULL` in the rent column and `NULL` again in the total. The rule is short: any arithmetic that touches a null produces a null. If you do not know the rent, you cannot know nine times the rent, and SQL refuses to invent a number. `595.00 + NULL` returns null for the same reason.

blocks.label: About those trailing zeros
blocks.text: The rents were stored as 610.00 and 725.00, but this page's SQLite engine prints them as 610 and 725, while MySQL prints 610.00 and 725.00. Only the display differs; the stored value is identical, and every comparison and total in this lesson is unaffected.
Nulls in comparisons split your data
The unknown answer bites hardest in ordinary comparisons that have nothing to do with nulls. Ask StayWell for the out-of-state students with the home state still cleared on S003.

One row comes back: S002 Carter PA. S003 is missing from the list -- not because the student is known to live in Ohio, but because the comparison could not be answered. A row with no value is excluded by `= 'OH'` and excluded by `<> 'OH'` at the same time.
The same thing happens with numbers. Count the rooms above and below a 500.00 rent line.

The first count is 3 and the second is 1. ROOM holds 5 rows, and 3 plus 1 is 4. The unpriced room fell out of both halves. Whenever two opposite filters fail to add up to the row count, look for nulls first.
Nulls inside aggregate functions
Aggregate functions do not fail on nulls, they skip them, and the skipping is where reports go wrong. Run all four numbers at once.

SELECT COUNT(*) AS ALL_ROOMS,
       COUNT(MONTHLY_RENT) AS RENTS_RECORDED,
       SUM(MONTHLY_RENT) AS TOTAL_RENT,
       AVG(MONTHLY_RENT) AS AVERAGE_RENT
FROM ROOM;

You get 5, 4, 2380 and 595. `COUNT(*)` counted all five rows because it counts rows, not values. `COUNT(MONTHLY_RENT)` counted the four rooms that have a rent. `SUM` added those same four. And `AVG` divided 2380 by 4, not by 5, so it reported 595. If you had assumed five rooms you would have expected 476, and been off by 119 dollars a month.

blocks.label: Say which count you mean
blocks.text: "How many rooms are there?" and "how many rooms have a rent on file?" are different questions with different answers, and `COUNT(*)` and `COUNT(MONTHLY_RENT)` answer them separately. Before you put a number in front of anyone, decide which question you are answering and pick the matching form.

blocks.starter:
-- Step 1: clear one home state so there is a null to study.
UPDATE STUDENT
SET HOME_STATE = NULL
WHERE STUDENT_ID = 'S003';

-- Step 2: this is meant to list the students whose home state is missing.
-- Run the box exactly as written first. No result table will appear at all,
-- because the condition below matches nothing. Then repair the condition.
SELECT STUDENT_ID, LAST_NAME, HOME_STATE
FROM STUDENT
WHERE HOME_STATE = NULL;
blocks.hint: Run it unchanged first. The page answers "Statement ran. 1 row affected." -- that 1 belongs to the UPDATE, and the absence of any result table is the SELECT matching nothing. Now swap the comparison for the null-aware test and you get a real grid: one row, S003, with NULL in HOME_STATE.

items: Test for a missing value with `IS NULL` or `IS NOT NULL`, because `= NULL` returns nothing at all.
Read a `NULL` in the result grid as "nothing recorded here" -- not as a zero, and not as an empty string.
Expect any arithmetic that touches a null to come back null, including multiplication and addition.
Remember that `<>` throws out the rows with no value, exactly as `=` does.
Decide between `COUNT(*)` and `COUNT(column)` before you report a number to anyone.
Read `AVG` as the average of the values that exist, not as the average of every row.

sections.title: Summary of SQL Clauses, Functions, and Operators

blocks.text: Everything in this module was one table at a time, and it all fits into six clauses, five aggregate functions and a short list of operators. This section is the reference page. You are not expected to memorize it in one sitting -- you are expected to come back to it while you write.
The six clauses

There are two orders that matter. The written order is the order you type the clauses in, and getting it wrong is a syntax error. The evaluated order is the order the database does the work in, and getting it wrong is a logic error.

blocks.caption: The clauses of a single-table query, in both orders
rows: Names the columns and computed values you want to see
Names the table the rows come from
Keeps or discards one row at a time
Collapses the surviving rows into one row per group
Arranges the finished rows for display

blocks.text: `SELECT` is the only clause a statement cannot do without -- `SELECT 595.00 + NULL;` is a complete statement in both engines -- but every query that reads a table needs `FROM` as well. The remaining four are optional, and when you use them they have to appear in the written order above.

The gap between the two orders explains two rules that otherwise look arbitrary. An aggregate function cannot appear in `WHERE`, because `WHERE` runs before any group exists; both engines refuse it, and SQLite words the complaint "misuse of aggregate". And an alias you invent in `SELECT` is meant for `ORDER BY` rather than for `WHERE`, because `ORDER BY` runs after the SELECT list is built while `WHERE` runs before it.

blocks.label: Where the engines differ: an alias in WHERE
blocks.text: MySQL rejects `SELECT ITEM_ID, PRICE * 2 AS DOUBLED FROM ITEM WHERE DOUBLED > 60;` with "Unknown column 'DOUBLED' in 'where clause'". The SQLite engine on this page accepts it as an extension and returns AV07 and CF21, so a query that runs here can still fail on a MySQL server. Repeat the whole expression -- `WHERE PRICE * 2 > 60` -- and it works in both.

SELECT CATEGORY, COUNT(*) AS ITEM_COUNT, AVG(PRICE) AS AVERAGE_PRICE
FROM ITEM
WHERE ON_HAND > 10
GROUP BY CATEGORY
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY CATEGORY;

Against KimTay's five items that query returns exactly one row: Habitat, 2, 46.37. All five items pass `ON_HAND > 10`, they fall into four categories, and Habitat is the only category holding more than one item, so `HAVING` discards the other three groups. Remove the `HAVING` line and four rows come back instead.
The aggregate functions

Each of these collapses many rows into a single number. There are five of them, in six forms, because `COUNT` comes in two: `COUNT(*)` and `COUNT(column)`. Every form except `COUNT(*)` ignores nulls, which is the detail that turns an aggregate into a wrong report.

blocks.caption: Aggregate functions and how each one treats a missing value
rows: The number of rows, whatever those rows contain
The number of rows where that column holds a value
The total of the values present in that column
The total divided by the number of values present
Skips nulls in the total and in the divisor

blocks.text: Run `SELECT MIN(PRICE), MAX(PRICE), SUM(ON_HAND), COUNT(*) FROM ITEM;` against KimTay and you get 11.99, 64.99, 235 and 5. Every ITEM row is filled in, so nothing is skipped and the four numbers describe all five items.
The operators

Operators are what you build conditions out of. The comparison and logical operators came from Module 3 and lesson 4-1; `BETWEEN`, `LIKE`, `IN`, and `IS NULL` were added across this module. The examples below are written against KimTay's ITEM and CUSTOMER tables.

blocks.caption: Operators you can use in a condition
rows: A value is smaller, or smaller or equal
A value is larger, or larger or equal
Both conditions hold for the same row
At least one of the conditions holds
A value falls inside an inclusive range
Text matches a pattern built with % and _
A value appears somewhere in a list
No value is recorded in the column
Some value is recorded in the column

blocks.text: Those ten examples match, in order: CF21; the other four items; AV07; AV07 and CF21; FT88; CF21 and GR15; CF21, DG04 and GR15; CF21, FT88 and GR15; customer 1310 Companion Care Clinic; and customers 1120, 1310 and 1420. None of the fragments carries an `ORDER BY`, so the order the rows actually appear in is the engine's choice -- the item IDs are simply listed alphabetically here. The two null tests are written against StayWell's ROOM table, where `IS NULL` finds nothing and `IS NOT NULL` finds all five rooms until you clear a rent yourself, because every seeded room has one.

blocks.label: Where the engines differ: text and decimals
blocks.text: Case sensitivity in `LIKE` depends on the product and its collation. This page's SQLite ignores case for ordinary letters, so `LIKE 'comp%'` still finds Companion Care Clinic, while MySQL follows the column's collation -- decide the case yourself rather than relying on either default. Decimal display also varies: a rent stored as 610.00 prints as 610 in this page's engine and as 610.00 in MySQL, and the stored value is identical either way.

cards.title: Written order is not working order
cards.body: You write SELECT first, but the database reads FROM and WHERE first and builds your output columns near the end. When a clause complains about something that looks perfectly defined, ask whether that thing exists yet at the moment the clause runs.

cards.title: A missing value is not a small value
cards.body: A null does not compare as zero, and COUNT(column) never counts one. In both this page's SQLite and in MySQL an ascending ORDER BY puts nulls ahead of every real value rather than treating them as low numbers. Any column created without NOT NULL can hold one, so check it with IS NULL before you trust a total, an average or a percentage built on it.

blocks.text: A checklist for any single-table query

items: Name the one table in `FROM`, then decide what a single row must satisfy in `WHERE`.
Add `GROUP BY` only when you want one row per group instead of one row per record.
Put conditions about individual rows in `WHERE` and conditions about group totals in `HAVING`.
Repeat the full expression in `WHERE` instead of the alias you gave it in `SELECT`, so the query runs on both engines.
Put `ORDER BY` last, and name a tie-breaker column when the first sort column repeats.
Test any column that is allowed to be empty with `IS NULL` before you trust an average or a count.
Run it, read the row count out loud, and ask whether that number is believable for this business.

quizzes.heading: Knowledge check: what a missing value does to your query

questions.stem: StayWell's housing office clears the HOME_STATE on one STUDENT row until the student re-verifies it, then runs `SELECT STUDENT_ID FROM STUDENT WHERE HOME_STATE = NULL;` and gets no rows back at all. What went wrong?
options: The STUDENT table holds no missing home states, so an empty result is the honest answer
SQL stops with a syntax error, because NULL cannot appear on the right of an operator
Comparing any value to NULL produces unknown, and WHERE keeps only rows that test true
The equals sign compares numbers only, so a two-character state code can never match
optionNotes: The row was cleared on purpose, so a missing home state does exist and the empty result is wrong.
The statement is legal SQL and runs without complaint, which is exactly what makes the empty result dangerous.
Right - a null is an unknown, an unknown compared with anything stays unknown, and WHERE discards everything that is not true.
The equals sign compares text as readily as numbers, as in `HOME_STATE = 'OH'`, so the data type is not the problem.
questions.takeaway: Write `IS NULL`, because `= NULL` evaluates to unknown on every row and therefore returns nothing.

questions.stem: Room 202 at Sycamore Court is being reconfigured and its MONTHLY_RENT has been cleared. The housing office counts the rooms renting above 500.00 and gets 3, counts the rooms at 500.00 or less and gets 1, and expected the two to add up to the 5 rows in ROOM. What happened?
options: The room with no recorded rent fails both tests, so it lands in neither count
COUNT(*) discards any row that holds a null in any column of the table
The two queries share overlapping rows, so one room was counted in both results
The engine rounds 500.00 differently in each query, pushing one room out of both
optionNotes: Right - both `> 500.00` and `<= 500.00` evaluate to unknown against a missing rent, so that row survives neither filter.
`COUNT(*)` counts rows whatever they contain; it was `WHERE` that removed the row before counting began.
The two conditions are opposites, so no room can satisfy both and double counting is impossible.
Both queries compare against the same literal in the same engine, and rounding plays no part in the missing row.
questions.takeaway: A row with a null sits outside both halves of a comparison, so opposite filters do not add up to the table's row count.

questions.scenarioTitle: The average rent that looks too high
questions.stem: With room 202's rent still cleared, a StayWell report runs `SELECT SUM(MONTHLY_RENT), AVG(MONTHLY_RENT) FROM ROOM;` The sum is 2380 and ROOM holds 5 rows, so the reader expects an average near 476, but AVG returns 595. Which explanation is correct?
options: AVG rounded its result up to the nearest five dollars before returning it
AVG treated the null as zero, and that zero pulled the reported average upward
AVG used only the Millbrook Commons rooms, because those rows are stored first
AVG ignored the row with no rent and divided 2380 by the four recorded rents
optionNotes: AVG did no rounding here; 2380 divided by 4 is exactly 595, with nothing left over.
A null counted as zero would drag the average down toward 476 rather than up to 595.
AVG reads every row the WHERE clause allows through, and this query has no WHERE clause at all.
Right - AVG skips nulls in the total and in the divisor, so it divided by 4 instead of by 5.
questions.takeaway: AVG is the average of the values that exist, so report `COUNT(column)` next to it whenever the column can be empty.

blocks.text: Module 4 stayed inside one table on purpose. Every question you asked -- which rows, which columns, in what order, summarized how -- was answered without a join, because most real reporting work starts exactly there. You added ten new tools to the `SELECT` you already had: compound conditions, `BETWEEN`, computed columns, `LIKE`, `IN`, multi-column sorting, aggregate functions, `DISTINCT`, subqueries, and `GROUP BY` with `HAVING`.

items: You can name the columns you want in the `SELECT` list, and use `*` only when you truly want all of them.
You can filter rows with a simple condition and combine conditions with `AND`, `OR`, and `NOT`, knowing `AND` is evaluated first.
You know `BETWEEN` tests a range and counts both endpoints as matches.
You can build a computed column such as `ON_HAND * PRICE` and give it a readable heading with `AS`.
You can search text with `LIKE` using the `%` and `_` wildcards.
You can replace a long chain of `OR` tests with `IN` and a list of values.
You can sort on more than one column, with a major sort key and a minor sort key, and reverse either one with `DESC`.
You can count, total, average, and find extremes with `COUNT`, `SUM`, `AVG`, `MAX`, and `MIN`.
You know an aggregate function returns one row for the whole table unless you group.
You can strip repeated values out of a result with `DISTINCT`.
You can nest one query inside another and let the inner result feed the outer condition.
You can group rows with `GROUP BY` and get one summary row per group.
You can filter groups with `HAVING`, and explain why that is not the same as `WHERE`.
You still have `IS NULL` from Module 3 for testing missing values, because `NULL` is never equal to anything.

blocks.text: The clause order that never changes
Whatever the query, the clauses are written in one fixed order. Leave any of them out, but never reorder them. This statement uses all six of them on the KimTay `ITEM` table:

SELECT CATEGORY, COUNT(*) AS NUM_ITEMS
FROM ITEM
WHERE PRICE > 12
GROUP BY CATEGORY
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 1
ORDER BY NUM_ITEMS DESC, CATEGORY;

That returns three rows: `Habitat` with 2, then `Food` with 1, then `Grooming` with 1. The `HAVING` test here is deliberately generous -- every group that forms has at least one row, so nothing is thrown away after grouping. `Accessory` is missing for a different reason: the 11.99 leash was removed by `WHERE` before any grouping happened. The tie between `Food` and `Grooming` is broken alphabetically by the second sort key.

blocks.label: Written order is not run order
blocks.text: You write `SELECT` first, but the database works through the clauses in this order: `FROM`, then `WHERE`, then `GROUP BY`, then `HAVING`, then `SELECT`, then `ORDER BY`. That single fact explains why `WHERE` cannot test a group total while `HAVING` can, and why `ORDER BY` -- the last clause to run -- can sort by a column alias, while `WHERE` runs long before that alias exists.

blocks.label: Two engines, two small surprises
blocks.text: The sandbox on this page runs SQLite; Module 3 taught MySQL. Almost everything in this module behaves identically in both, but watch two things. First, money: MySQL's `DECIMAL` arithmetic is exact, while SQLite calculates in binary floating point, so `SELECT AVG(PRICE) FROM ITEM;` shows `32.496` under MySQL and `32.495999999999995` here, and `15 * 64.99` shows `974.85` there and `974.8499999999999` here. The stored data is identical -- only the arithmetic display differs, and the extra digits are noise, not a wrong answer. Second, aliases: SQLite lets you use a `SELECT` alias inside `WHERE`, MySQL does not, so repeat the expression instead of the alias and the same query runs on both.

blocks.starter:
SELECT CATEGORY, COUNT(*) AS NUM_ITEMS, AVG(PRICE) AS AVG_PRICE
FROM ITEM
WHERE PRICE BETWEEN 10 AND 70
GROUP BY CATEGORY
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY AVG_PRICE DESC;
blocks.solution:
SELECT CATEGORY, COUNT(*) AS NUM_ITEMS, AVG(PRICE) AS AVG_PRICE
FROM ITEM
WHERE PRICE BETWEEN 10 AND 70
GROUP BY CATEGORY
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 1
ORDER BY AVG_PRICE DESC;
blocks.hint: Run it as written -- one row, Habitat with 2 items averaging 46.37. Then change `HAVING COUNT(*) > 1` to `>= 1` and the other three categories reappear, in the order Habitat, Food, Grooming, Accessory.

blocks.text: The next module lifts the one-table restriction for good. You met a basic join back in Module 3; from here on you will pull columns from several tables in a single statement and see how the pieces fit together. Everything in this module carries over unchanged: the same `WHERE`, the same sorting, the same aggregates, applied to a wider set of rows.

These are the words your instructor, the textbook, and the error messages will use. Read the definition, then say the term out loud against a query you have already run -- the vocabulary sticks faster when it is attached to something you typed.
Choosing rows and columns

blocks.caption: Module 4 key terms: filtering and selecting
rows: A single comparison of one column against a value or another column, such as `BALANCE > 1000`.
Two or more simple conditions joined with `AND` or `OR`, or reversed with `NOT`.
An operator that tests whether a value falls inside a range, counting both endpoints as matches.
A column that is not stored in the table but calculated for each row, such as `ON_HAND * PRICE`.
A temporary name given to a column or expression so the result carries a readable heading.

An operator that compares text against a pattern instead of against an exact value. By default both SQLite and MySQL match ordinary ASCII letters without regard to case, so `'%Pet%'` and `'%pet%'` return the same rows here.
A character inside a `LIKE` pattern that stands for other characters: `%` for any number of them, `_` for exactly one.
An operator that tests whether a value appears somewhere in a list, replacing a chain of `OR` tests.
The only correct test for a missing value, because `NULL` is never equal to anything, including another `NULL`.

blocks.text: Sorting, summarizing, and grouping

blocks.caption: Module 4 key terms: ordering and aggregating
rows: The column named in `ORDER BY` that decides the order of the rows.
When you sort on two columns, the first is the major key and the second breaks ties inside it.
Direction keywords; ascending is the default, and `DESC` applies only to the column it follows.
A function that collapses many rows into one value: `COUNT`, `SUM`, `AVG`, `MAX`, `MIN`.
A keyword that removes repeated values from a result so each one appears once.
A query written inside another query; the inner one runs first and the outer one uses its result.
Collecting rows that share a value so an aggregate can be computed once per group.
The clause that names the column whose equal values define the groups.
The clause that filters whole groups after grouping, the way `WHERE` filters individual rows before it.

blocks.label: The one pair students mix up
blocks.text: `WHERE` tests one row at a time and runs before any grouping; `HAVING` tests a finished group and runs after. If your condition mentions `COUNT`, `SUM`, or `AVG`, it belongs in `HAVING`. If it mentions a plain column value, put it in `WHERE`, where it removes rows early and keeps the groups honest.

blocks.solution:
SELECT CATEGORY, COUNT(*) AS NUM_ITEMS
FROM ITEM
GROUP BY CATEGORY
ORDER BY CATEGORY;
blocks.hint: The starter returns four rows -- Accessory, Food, Grooming, Habitat. The worked answer groups instead of de-duplicating, so you also see that Habitat holds 2 items and the rest hold 1.

blocks.text: Ten questions covering the whole module. Several of them hand you a finished statement and ask what it returns against the KimTay and StayWell data you have been using all along -- reading SQL is half of writing it.

blocks.label: How to read a statement you did not write
blocks.text: Work through it the way the database does. Start at `FROM` to see which table is in play, apply `WHERE` to see which rows survive, apply `GROUP BY` and `HAVING` if they are there, then build the `SELECT` list, and only then put the rows in `ORDER BY` order. Predict the row count before you predict the values.

Answer from the data first, then confirm. Guessing and checking teaches you far less than deciding on an answer, running the statement, and finding out exactly where your reasoning went sideways. If a total or an average comes back with a long tail of decimal digits, that is the SQLite floating-point display noted in the module summary, not a mistake in your query.

blocks.text: KimTay Pet Supplies

Exercise 1. The warehouse manager wants a price list of items costing between 15 and 50 dollars, most expensive first, showing `ITEM_ID`, `DESCRIPTION`, and `PRICE`. Expect 3 rows, beginning with the grain-free food at 42.50 and ending with the grooming kit at 15.25.

Exercise 2. Marketing wants every customer whose name mentions pets in any form, showing `CUSTOMER_NUM` and `CUSTOMER_NAME`. Use `LIKE` rather than typing the names in yourself. Expect 2 rows: Access Pet Center and Downtown Aquarium & Pets.
Exercise 3. The bookkeeper wants a single row holding two numbers: how many customers KimTay has, and the total of their balances. Expect 4 and 9533.25. Give both columns readable headings with `AS`.

Exercise 4. Which items cost more than the average item price? Use a subquery so the average is computed by the database, not pasted in by you. Sort most expensive first. Expect 2 rows -- the aviary cage at 64.99 and the grain-free food at 42.50 -- because the five prices average 32.496. Run `SELECT AVG(PRICE) FROM ITEM;` on its own and this sandbox prints `32.495999999999995`, which is the same number shown the way SQLite's binary floating point stores it.

Exercise 5. Show each rep number with the number of customers assigned to it, keeping only reps carrying more than one customer. Expect a single row: rep 20 with 2 customers. Decide deliberately whether that last condition belongs in `WHERE` or `HAVING`.
StayWell Student Accommodation
Exercise 6. List every room type with its lowest and highest monthly rent, room type in alphabetical order. Expect 3 rows: Double at 450 and 465, Single at 595 and 610, Studio at 725 and 725.

Exercise 7. For each property, count its rooms and average their rent, keeping only properties with more than two rooms. Expect one row: P200, 3 rooms, average rent 600. Millbrook Commons drops out because it has only two rooms in the sample.

Exercise 8. List the first name, last name, and home state of every student from Ohio or Michigan, sorted by last name, using `IN` instead of two `OR` tests. Expect 3 rows in the order Ibrahim, Nguyen, Park.

items: Every query works from a single table -- no joins are needed anywhere in this module.
Your row counts match the counts stated in each exercise before you look at the values.
Any condition mentioning `COUNT`, `SUM`, or `AVG` sits in `HAVING`, not `WHERE`.
Computed and aggregated columns carry a readable heading supplied with `AS`.
Text values are wrapped in straight single quotes and numbers are not quoted at all.
You repeated the expression in `WHERE` rather than the alias, so the query would also run under MySQL.

blocks.label: Save the work
blocks.text: Put all eight statements in one `.sql` script the way Module 3 showed, with a comment line above each one naming the exercise. That file becomes your own reference, and rerunning it end to end is the fastest way to prove nothing you wrote depends on a table you edited earlier.

questions.scenarioTitle: Naming the parts of one WHERE clause
questions.stem: KimTay's bookkeeper writes `SELECT CUSTOMER_NAME FROM CUSTOMER WHERE BALANCE > 1000 AND CITY = 'Maple Grove';` and gets back one row, Access Pet Center. Using this module's vocabulary, what is that `WHERE` clause?
options: A simple condition, because it appears once in the statement and names one table.
A computed column, because the database has to work out whether each row qualifies.
A grouping, because it collects the Maple Grove rows together before they are counted.
A compound condition, because two simple conditions are joined together by AND.
optionNotes: A simple condition is a single comparison; this clause contains two of them joined together.
A computed column produces a value in the result, such as ON_HAND * PRICE, not a true-or-false test.
Grouping happens only when GROUP BY is present, and this statement has no GROUP BY at all.
Right -- BALANCE > 1000 and CITY = 'Maple Grove' are each simple conditions, and AND makes the pair compound.
questions.takeaway: One comparison is a simple condition; two or more joined by AND, OR, or NOT make a compound condition.

questions.scenarioTitle: One value per row, or one value in total
questions.stem: The warehouse manager runs `SELECT DESCRIPTION, ON_HAND * PRICE AS VALUE_ON_HAND FROM ITEM;` and gets five rows, then runs `SELECT SUM(ON_HAND * PRICE) AS TOTAL_VALUE FROM ITEM;` and gets 5621.65 in a single row. Which sentence names the difference correctly?
options: The first uses an alias and the second does not, which is why one row comes back.
The first is a computed column giving one value per row; the second adds an aggregate function.
The second is a subquery, because the multiplication sits nested inside the SUM call.
Both are aggregate functions, but the second is narrowed by a hidden HAVING clause.
optionNotes: Both statements use AS; an alias renames a column and has no effect on how many rows return.
Right -- ON_HAND * PRICE is computed once per row, and SUM collapses those five values into one.
A subquery is a complete SELECT nested inside another statement, which is not what an expression inside SUM is.
The first statement has no aggregate function, and neither statement contains a HAVING clause.
questions.takeaway: A computed column returns one value per row; an aggregate function returns one value for the whole group.

quizzes.heading: Module 4 cumulative review: reading and writing single-table queries

questions.scenarioTitle: The customer list that came back three long
questions.stem: KimTay's bookkeeper runs `SELECT CUSTOMER_NAME FROM CUSTOMER WHERE CITY = 'Maple Grove' OR CITY = 'Brookville' AND BALANCE > 4000;` against the four sample customers. Which result is correct?
options: All four customers, because OR widens the search to include every city in the table.
Three names: Access Pet Center, Companion Care Clinic, and Whiskers & Wags Boutique.
Only Whiskers & Wags Boutique, because the balance test applies to every row in CUSTOMER.
Nothing at all, because one WHERE clause is not allowed to mix OR and AND together.
optionNotes: OR does not switch off the rest of the condition; Downtown Aquarium & Pets sits in Northfield and fails both branches.
Right -- AND is evaluated first, so the test reads: in Maple Grove, or else in Brookville with a balance over 4000.
The balance test belongs only to the Brookville branch, so both Maple Grove customers return regardless of balance.
Mixing AND and OR is legal; what you control with parentheses is which one is evaluated first.
questions.takeaway: AND binds tighter than OR, so add parentheses whenever you want the OR grouped first.

questions.scenarioTitle: Counting the shelves inside a range
questions.stem: The warehouse manager runs `SELECT ITEM_ID FROM ITEM WHERE ON_HAND BETWEEN 15 AND 30;`. The five stored ON_HAND values are 15, 48, 120, 30, and 22. What comes back?
options: Only GR15, because BETWEEN leaves out the two values that name the range.
Nothing, because BETWEEN works on dates and not on whole numbers.
Five rows, because BETWEEN checks the low value and ignores the high one.
Three rows -- AV07, FT88, and GR15 -- because both endpoints count as matches.
optionNotes: BETWEEN includes its endpoints, so the 15 on hand and the 30 on hand both qualify alongside 22.
BETWEEN works on any ordered type: numbers, text, and dates all compare the same way.
Both boundaries are tested, not just the low one, so 48 and 120 are excluded for exceeding the high value of 30.
Right -- 15, 30, and 22 all fall inside an inclusive range, while 48 and 120 sit above it.
questions.takeaway: BETWEEN 15 AND 30 means the same as ON_HAND >= 15 AND ON_HAND <= 30, endpoints included.

questions.stem: Marketing asks which KimTay customers mention pets. The query is `SELECT CUSTOMER_NAME FROM CUSTOMER WHERE CUSTOMER_NAME LIKE '%Pet%';`. What is the result against the four stored names?
options: Two rows: Access Pet Center and Downtown Aquarium & Pets.
One row, Access Pet Center, since Pets ends in an s and cannot match.
No rows, because a percent sign is allowed only at the end of a pattern.
All four rows, because LIKE returns everything once the pattern contains a wildcard.
optionNotes: Right -- the pattern means any characters, then Pet, then any characters, so Pets matches as well.
The trailing percent sign already covers that s, so Downtown Aquarium & Pets matches too.
A wildcard is legal at either end or in the middle; its position changes the meaning, not the legality.
LIKE still tests every row: Companion Care Clinic and Whiskers & Wags Boutique contain no Pet.
questions.takeaway: In a LIKE pattern, % stands for any number of characters, including none, and _ stands for exactly one.

questions.stem: Rep 20 and rep 35 both carry Maple Grove addresses. A clerk writes `SELECT CUSTOMER_NAME FROM CUSTOMER WHERE REP_NUM = (SELECT REP_NUM FROM REP WHERE CITY = 'Maple Grove');`. What is wrong with it?
options: Nothing is wrong; an equals sign accepts however many values the subquery hands back.
The subquery must become a join, because a subquery cannot read a second table.
The inner query returns two rep numbers, so the outer test needs IN instead of equals.
The subquery runs last, so the outer WHERE clause has nothing available to compare.
optionNotes: The engines disagree about how to punish it: MySQL stops with a subquery-returns-more-than-one-row error, while SQLite runs it quietly and compares against just one of the two values.
Reading REP is exactly the point of the subquery; the trouble is how many values come back from it.
Right -- IN accepts a list, so it covers rep 20 and rep 35 and returns all three of their customers.
The inner query runs first, and its result is precisely what the outer condition tests.
questions.takeaway: Use = only when a subquery is guaranteed to return one value; use IN whenever it can return several.

questions.scenarioTitle: Which shelves hold over a thousand dollars
questions.stem: The warehouse manager runs `SELECT ITEM_ID, ON_HAND * PRICE AS INVENTORY_VALUE FROM ITEM WHERE ON_HAND * PRICE > 1000;`. What does the result contain?
options: Every item, because a computed column is built for each row before any filter runs.
Nothing, because a column invented in the SELECT list cannot be tested by WHERE.
Only DG04, because 120 units is the largest quantity anywhere in the table.
Two rows: CF21, whose stock is worth 2040.00, and DG04, worth 1438.80.
optionNotes: The expression is computed for each row and then tested, so the three rows under 1000 are removed.
Repeating the expression in WHERE is always allowed; it is the alias name that is not portable there.
Quantity alone does not decide it: 15 aviary cages at 64.99 come to 974.85 and fall short.
Right -- 48 times 42.50 is 2040.00 and 120 times 11.99 is 1438.80, while the other three land below 1000. This sandbox prints them as 2040 and 1438.8.
questions.takeaway: Repeat the expression in WHERE rather than the alias -- SQLite accepts an alias there, MySQL does not.

questions.scenarioTitle: City counts after the zero balance drops out
questions.stem: Companion Care Clinic in Maple Grove carries a balance of 0.00. The bookkeeper runs `SELECT CITY, COUNT(*) AS NUM_CUSTOMERS FROM CUSTOMER WHERE BALANCE > 0 GROUP BY CITY ORDER BY CITY;`. What comes back?
options: Three rows, and Maple Grove shows 1, because WHERE removes rows before grouping.
Three rows, and Maple Grove shows 2, because grouping happens before the filter runs.
One row holding the total number of customers whose balance is above zero.
An error, because COUNT is not allowed unless every column appears in GROUP BY.
optionNotes: Right -- the clinic is filtered out first, so Maple Grove has one surviving row to count.
WHERE runs before GROUP BY, so the zero-balance clinic never reaches the Maple Grove group.
GROUP BY produces one row per city, not one row overall; leaving it out would give a single total.
CITY is the only non-aggregated column and it appears in GROUP BY, so the statement is valid.
questions.takeaway: WHERE thins the rows before grouping, which changes every count, total, and average that follows.

questions.scenarioTitle: The rep carrying more than one account
questions.stem: KimTay's sales manager runs `SELECT REP_NUM, COUNT(*) AS NUM_CUSTOMERS FROM CUSTOMER GROUP BY REP_NUM HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;` against the four sample customers. What is the result?
options: Three rows, one per rep, because HAVING cannot remove a group once it has formed.
An error, because a condition on COUNT belongs in WHERE rather than in HAVING.
One row -- rep 20, with two customers assigned to it.
Two rows, because rep 20 and rep 65 each hold more than one customer.
optionNotes: Removing groups is exactly what HAVING does; only the group meeting the condition survives.
A condition on an aggregate must be in HAVING, because WHERE runs before the groups exist.
Right -- rep 20 holds Access Pet Center and Companion Care Clinic; reps 35 and 65 hold one each.
Rep 65 is on one account only, Whiskers & Wags Boutique, so that group is filtered out.
questions.takeaway: HAVING filters finished groups; a condition mentioning COUNT, SUM, or AVG can live nowhere else.

questions.scenarioTitle: Rent sheets for the leasing office
questions.stem: StayWell's leasing office runs `SELECT PROPERTY_ID, ROOM_NUM, MONTHLY_RENT FROM ROOM ORDER BY PROPERTY_ID, MONTHLY_RENT DESC;`. How do the five rooms come out?
options: Rents descending across both properties, so the 725.00 studio is the very first row.
P100 first with 595.00 above 450.00, then P200 with 725.00, 610.00, and 465.00.
P200 first, because DESC reverses the property order along with the rent order.
In whatever order the table stores them, because two sort keys cancel each other out.
optionNotes: PROPERTY_ID is the major sort key, so every P100 room is listed before any P200 room.
Right -- PROPERTY_ID sorts ascending as the major key, and DESC reverses only the rent inside each property.
DESC applies to the column it follows and to nothing else, so PROPERTY_ID stays ascending.
Two sort keys work together: the second one breaks the ties the first one leaves behind.
questions.takeaway: In ORDER BY, the first column is the major sort key and DESC attaches only to the column right before it.

questions.stem: KimTay stocks five items across four categories, with two of them in Habitat. What does `SELECT COUNT(*) AS NUM_ROWS, COUNT(DISTINCT CATEGORY) AS NUM_CATEGORIES FROM ITEM;` return?
options: 5 and 5, because COUNT(DISTINCT ...) counts rows the same way COUNT(*) does.
4 and 4, because both counts skip the second Habitat item as a duplicate row.
An error, because two aggregate functions cannot appear in one SELECT list.
5 and 4, because two items share the Habitat category and DISTINCT counts it once.
optionNotes: DISTINCT removes repeated values before counting, so the two Habitat rows contribute one category.
COUNT(*) counts every row without exception, so it reports 5 whatever the categories look like.
A SELECT list may hold as many aggregate functions as you need, each summarizing the same rows.
Right -- five rows exist, and Accessory, Food, Grooming, and Habitat make four distinct categories.
questions.takeaway: COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(DISTINCT column) counts how many different values that column holds.

questions.stem: The buyer runs `SELECT ITEM_ID, PRICE FROM ITEM WHERE PRICE > (SELECT AVG(PRICE) FROM ITEM);`. The five prices are 64.99, 42.50, 11.99, 27.75, and 15.25, which average 32.496 -- printed in this sandbox as 32.495999999999995. What comes back?
options: Two rows -- AV07 at 64.99 and CF21 at 42.50 -- the only prices above the average.
All five rows, because the inner query runs once per row and always matches.
No rows, because an aggregate function is not permitted inside a subquery.
Three rows, because the two Habitat items and the food item all beat the average.
optionNotes: Right -- the subquery produces the average once, and only the cage and the food price exceed it.
The subquery is evaluated once here and yields a single number the outer condition tests.
An aggregate inside a subquery is one of its most common uses, since it returns exactly one value.
FT88 is a Habitat item priced at 27.75, which sits below the average, so only two rows qualify.
questions.takeaway: A subquery lets the database compute a value such as an average and compare every row against it.

matchers.heading: Match the keyword to its definition
matchers.prompt: Click a keyword, then click the definition that belongs to it. Each keyword matches exactly one definition. If two feel close, ask what the keyword is testing: a range, a pattern, a list, a finished group, or repeated values.

zones.label: Tests against a list of values

cards.text: `BETWEEN`
cards.why: It tests whether a value falls between a low and a high value, counting both endpoints as matches.

cards.text: `LIKE`
cards.why: It compares text against a pattern rather than an exact value, which is why it needs wildcards.

cards.text: `IN`
cards.why: It checks whether a value appears in a list, replacing a long chain of OR comparisons.

cards.text: `HAVING`
cards.why: It runs after grouping, so it is the only clause that can test a group total such as COUNT(*).

cards.text: `DISTINCT`
cards.why: It strips duplicate values out of the result so each distinct value is listed one time.
